context: The Dual Monarchy of Austria-Hungary was formed by the 1867 Ausgleich (Compromise) between the Austrian Empire and the Kingdom of Hungary, uniting them under the shared Habsburg dynasty while each retained its own government.
adopted: The black-and-yellow Habsburg dynastic colors were used as the common flag from the 1867 compromise until the monarchy's dissolution at the end of World War I in 1918.
notes: This was the common/dynastic flag flown alongside, not instead of, Austria's and Hungary's own separate national flags.
disambiguation: Not to be confused with modern Austria's plain red-white-red horizontal triband, which predates the Habsburgs and was readopted after 1918.

polity: the Protectorate of Bohemia and Moravia
context: Established after Nazi Germany occupied the Czech rump state following the 1938 Munich Agreement and the 1939 dismemberment of Czechoslovakia, the Protectorate was a nominally autonomous puppet administration under a German Reichsprotektor.
adopted: Adopted in 1939 alongside the Protectorate's creation; it was abolished in 1945 when Czechoslovakia was restored at the end of World War II.
symbols: A blue triangular wedge (a truncated version of the Czechoslovak tricolor's hoist wedge) sits at the hoist, cut short so the German-controlled state flag deliberately echoes but does not fully reproduce the banned Czechoslovak national flag.
notes: Civil use in the Protectorate; state and party institutions flew the Nazi swastika flag alongside it.
disambiguation: Not to be confused with the full Czechoslovak tricolor (a complete blue hoist triangle over white-over-red), which this flag intentionally truncates.

context: Adopted in the late Qing dynasty's self-strengthening/modernization era as China's first formally adopted national flag, replacing the informal use of the imperial dragon banner for court purposes only.
adopted: Formally adopted in 1889 (with earlier informal naval use from the 1860s), remaining China's national flag until the Qing dynasty's fall in the 1911 Xinhai Revolution and the Republic's founding in 1912.
symbols: A single blue five-clawed dragon chasing a red flaming pearl, both centered on the yellow field.
disambiguation: Not to be confused with the five-colored Republican flag that replaced it in 1912, which drops the dragon entirely for five plain horizontal stripes.

context: Adopted at the founding of the Republic of China after the Qing dynasty's fall, the five stripes represented the "Five Races Under One Union" (Han, Manchu, Mongol, Hui, and Tibetan) the new republic claimed to unite.
adopted: Adopted in 1912 at the Republic's founding; superseded in 1928 when the Nationalist government's Northern Expedition unified the country under the Kuomintang's Blue Sky White Sun flag.
disambiguation: Not to be confused with the single-dragon Qing flag it replaced, or the red flag with blue canton adopted by the Nationalists in 1928.

context: Adopted by the Kuomintang-led Nationalist government upon the Northern Expedition's success in reunifying China under one government, based on the Kuomintang's own party flag first flown by Sun Yat-sen's revolutionary movement.
adopted: Adopted nationally in 1928, remaining the Republic of China's flag through the Nationalist mainland government's defeat in the Chinese Civil War in 1949 (it remains in use today on Taiwan).
symbols: A white twelve-pointed sun, representing progress, centered in a blue canton occupying the upper hoist quarter.
aliases: Blue Sky, White Sun, and a Wholly Red Earth
disambiguation: Not to be confused with the five-striped early Republican flag it replaced, or the People's Republic of China's later red flag with five gold stars.

context: Adopted upon German unification under Prussian leadership after the Franco-Prussian War, combining Prussia's black-and-white with the red-and-white of the Hanseatic cities to signal a Prussian-led but broader German union.
adopted: Adopted in 1871 at the Empire's founding; abolished in 1918 with the Kaiser's abdication and the founding of the Weimar Republic, which adopted black-red-gold instead.
disambiguation: Not to be confused with the Weimar Republic's black-red-gold tricolor, or Nazi Germany's later red flag with a black swastika on a white disc.

context: Adopted after the Nazi Party's 1933 seizure of power, replacing the Weimar Republic's tricolor and formally merging the state flag with the Nazi Party's own banner under the 1935 Reich Flag Law.
adopted: The party banner flew alongside the Weimar tricolor from 1933, becoming the sole national flag in 1935; abolished in 1945 with Germany's defeat in World War II.
layout: red field with disc and symbol
symbols: A white disc centered on the red field, bearing a black swastika rotated 45 degrees.
disambiguation: Not to be confused with the German Empire's black-white-red horizontal tricolor, which shares the same three colors but no swastika.

context: Created by the 1919 Treaty of Versailles as a semi-autonomous city-state under League of Nations protection, separating the majority-German port city from both Germany and the new Poland.
adopted: Adopted in 1920 upon the Free City's establishment; ceased use in 1939 when Nazi Germany annexed the city at the start of World War II.
symbols: A gold crown at the top, above two white Latin crosses stacked vertically beneath it — the city's traditional civic arms.
disambiguation: Not to be confused with the modern Polish city of Gdańsk's civic flag, which occupies the same location but uses a different, simpler crowned-cross design.

context: Readopted when the Bourbon monarchy was restored under Alfonso XII after the collapse of the short-lived First Spanish Republic, returning to Spain's traditional red-yellow-red naval colors dating to Charles III.
adopted: Readopted in 1875 with the Restoration; replaced in 1931 when King Alfonso XIII left Spain and the Second Republic adopted a purple-yellow-red tricolor instead.
layout: horizontal triband with coat of arms
symbols: The royal coat of arms, crowned and flanked by the Pillars of Hercules, positioned off-center toward the hoist on the yellow band.
disambiguation: Not to be confused with the Second Republic's red-yellow-purple tricolor, or Francoist Spain's later version of this same red-yellow-red flag bearing a different, eagle-crested coat of arms.

context: Adopted when King Alfonso XIII left Spain following municipal elections favoring republican candidates, the new tricolor deliberately broke from the monarchy's red-yellow-red by adding a purple band recalling Castile's historic republican/Comunero associations.
adopted: Adopted in 1931 at the Republic's proclamation; superseded in 1939 by Francisco Franco's Nationalist government after its victory in the Spanish Civil War.
symbols: Republican-era versions sometimes bore a mural crown and the Pillars of Hercules centered on the yellow band; the plain civil version carried no emblem.
notes: Civil flag flown plain; state and war versions added the republican coat of arms.
disambiguation: Not to be confused with the monarchist/Francoist red-yellow-red flag, which replaces the purple band with a second red one.

context: Adopted by Francisco Franco's Nationalist faction during the Spanish Civil War as a deliberate return to the monarchy's red-yellow-red colors, rejecting the Republic's purple band, with a new eagle-bearing coat of arms proclaiming the Nationalist cause.
adopted: Adopted in 1938 while the Civil War was still underway, remaining Spain's flag after the Nationalist victory in 1939; this specific eagle emblem was in use until a 1945 revision, with the wider red-yellow-red basic pattern continuing under Franco until his death in 1975.
layout: horizontal triband with coat of arms
symbols: The "eagle of Saint John" — a black eagle displayed, bearing a shield with the arms of the old Spanish kingdoms, the yoke-and-arrows Falangist emblem, and a scroll reading "UNA GRANDE LIBRE" — centered on the yellow band.
disambiguation: Not to be confused with the pre-1931 Restoration flag's crowned-and-pillared coat of arms, which sits on the same red-yellow-red base but with a different emblem.

context: Hungary's red-white-green tricolor with the historic Hungarian coat of arms was flown by the Kingdom of Hungary under Regent Miklós Horthy, a monarchy that after World War I kept the royal title and arms without an actual reigning king.
adopted: The coat-of-arms state flag dates to 1915; under Horthy's regency from 1920 it represented the officially still-monarchical state until the monarchy was formally abolished with the 1946 declaration of the republic.
layout: horizontal tricolor with coat of arms
symbols: The Hungarian coat of arms — a shield of red-and-white Árpád stripes beside a triple mound bearing a patriarchal cross, topped by the Holy Crown of Saint Stephen — centered on the white band.
disambiguation: Not to be confused with the plain red-white-green civil tricolor with no coat of arms, still used as Hungary's flag today.

context: Formalized after Persia's 1906 Constitutional Revolution, when the Qajar shahs granted a constitution and standardized state symbols including the flag's long-used Lion and Sun emblem.
adopted: Standardized in 1907 following the constitutional reforms; the Qajar dynasty and this flag ended in 1925 when Reza Khan founded the Pahlavi dynasty (which kept the same Lion and Sun on a similar tricolor).
symbols: A gold lion holding a scimitar, with a sun rising behind it, centered on the white band.
disambiguation: Not to be confused with the later Pahlavi-era version of the same Lion and Sun tricolor (a more standardized emblem), or modern Iran's post-1980 flag, which replaces the lion with the stylized Allah emblem.

context: Adopted when the Kingdom of Sardinia-Piedmont completed the unification of Italy under the House of Savoy, adding the Savoy royal coat of arms to the existing Italian tricolor used by the unification movement.
adopted: Adopted in 1861 at the Kingdom's proclamation; the coat of arms was dropped in 1946 when Italy voted to abolish the monarchy and become a republic.
layout: vertical tricolor with coat of arms
symbols: The crowned Savoy shield — a white cross on a red field, encircled by the collar of the Order of the Annunziata — centered on the white band.
disambiguation: Not to be confused with modern Italy's plain green-white-red tricolor, which is the same flag with the royal coat of arms removed.

context: Created by the Empire of Japan as a nominally independent state in occupied Manchuria, installing the deposed last Qing emperor Puyi as head of state to lend the puppet regime a veneer of legitimacy.
adopted: Adopted in 1932 at Manchukuo's founding; abolished in 1945 when Soviet forces invaded Manchuria at the end of World War II.
symbols: A canton in the upper hoist corner containing three narrow horizontal stripes — red, blue, white, then black — over the main yellow field.
notes: The yellow field and five colors echoed the earlier Republican Chinese five-race flag's palette, recast to claim harmony among Manchukuo's Japanese, Han, Manchu, Mongol, and Korean populations under Japanese direction.
disambiguation: Not to be confused with the earlier Republic of China five-striped flag (equal horizontal bands, no yellow field or canton) or the Qing dynasty's yellow dragon flag (a single dragon, no stripes).

context: Adopted by Sultan Hassan I as Morocco's first formally defined national flag, a plain red field in the long-standing Sharifian/Alaouite dynastic color, used before the French and Spanish protectorates were imposed in 1912.
adopted: Adopted around 1873 and confirmed in continued use through the years leading up to the 1912 protectorate treaties; superseded in 1915 when Sultan Yusef added the green pentagram (Seal of Solomon) still used today.
disambiguation: Not to be confused with modern Morocco's flag, which is this same red field with a green five-pointed star added in the center.

polity: the Xibei San Ma / Ma Clique
context: The "Xibei San Ma" (Three Ma's of the Northwest) were a group of allied Hui Muslim warlord families who governed Gansu, Ningxia, and Qinghai provinces during China's Warlord Era and the subsequent Nationalist period, nominally loyal to but effectively autonomous from the central government.
adopted: In informal use through the 1920s-1940s as a factional/military banner of the Ma family cliques' forces rather than a state-issued flag; it fell out of use with the Communist victory in the region in 1949.
symbols: A white crescent moon opening toward the fly with a small white five-pointed star beside it, both near the hoist — Islamic symbols marking the Ma cliques' Hui Muslim identity.
notes: A swallow-tailed/triangular pennant rather than a rectangular flag, typical of Chinese regional military banners of the period.
disambiguation: Not to be confused with the Ottoman Empire's rectangular red flag with crescent and star, which uses the same symbols in a different shape and arrangement.

context: Standardized during the Tanzimat reform era, when the Ottoman state modernized its institutions and symbols along European lines while retaining Islamic emblems reflecting the sultan's religious authority.
adopted: Adopted in 1844; remained in use until the Ottoman Empire's dissolution in 1922-1923 and its replacement by the Republic of Turkey's flag, which is nearly identical in design.
symbols: A white crescent moon opening toward the fly, with a white five-pointed star near the hoist side of the crescent's opening.
disambiguation: Not to be confused with modern Turkey's flag, which standardizes the exact size and placement of the same crescent and star; also distinct from Tunisia's crescent-and-star inside a white disc, or Morocco's green pentagram.

context: Adopted when the Principality of Romania was elevated to a kingdom under Carol I of the Hohenzollern-Sigmaringen dynasty, adding the royal coat of arms to the existing blue-yellow-red tricolor used since the 1859 union of Moldavia and Wallachia.
adopted: Adopted in 1881 at the Kingdom's proclamation; the coat of arms was dropped in 1947 when the monarchy was abolished and Romania became a people's republic.
layout: vertical tricolor with coat of arms
symbols: The royal coat of arms, topped with the Steel Crown of Romania and held by two supporters, centered on the yellow band.
disambiguation: Not to be confused with modern Romania's plain blue-yellow-red tricolor (no coat of arms) or Chad's nearly identical blue-yellow-red tricolor, which uses a slightly different, darker blue.

context: Formally confirmed as the Russian Empire's national flag by Nicholas II shortly before his coronation, adopting a merchant-marine tricolor with roots back to Peter the Great over the black-yellow-white imperial flag that had briefly competed with it.
adopted: Confirmed as the sole national flag in 1896; it was abolished after the February and October Revolutions of 1917 and replaced by Soviet Russia's red flag.
disambiguation: Not to be confused with the Netherlands' red-white-blue tricolor (different color order) or Slovenia's/Slovakia's tricolors, which add a coat of arms to a similarly-ordered white-blue-red base.

polity: the Emirate of Nejd (early House of Saud)
context: Flown by Ibn Saud's Emirate of Nejd after he recaptured Riyadh from the rival Al Rashid family in 1902, the start of the campaign that would eventually unify the peninsula into the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia in 1932.
adopted: In use from the 1902 reconquest of Riyadh until the Emirate was reorganized as the Sultanate of Nejd in 1921, part of the continuous evolution of Al Saud state flags that eventually produced the modern Saudi flag.
symbols: The Islamic shahada ("There is no god but God; Muhammad is the messenger of God") in white Arabic script across the field, with two crossed swords beneath it.
notes: War/state flag of the Al Saud emirate rather than a flag for civil or merchant use.
disambiguation: Not to be confused with the modern Saudi flag, which places a single sword (not crossed swords) beneath the shahada.

context: Adopted following the 1922 formation of the USSR from the constituent Soviet republics, built around the plain red flag of the Bolshevik revolution with the hammer and sickle added to symbolize the worker-peasant alliance.
adopted: Adopted in 1923 (with this specific proportion and star-placement standardized further by 1936); superseded in 1955 by a revised version with a thinner emblem, and ultimately retired with the Soviet Union's 1991 dissolution.
symbols: A gold hammer and sickle in the upper hoist area, with a gold-bordered red five-pointed star above them.
disambiguation: Not to be confused with the plain red flags of other communist movements with no hammer-and-sickle emblem, or the similar but differently-proportioned 1955 revision.

context: Adopted when the Principality of Serbia was elevated to a kingdom under Milan I Obrenovic after Serbia secured full independence from the Ottoman Empire at the 1878 Congress of Berlin.
adopted: Adopted in 1882 at the Kingdom's proclamation; superseded in 1918 when Serbia joined the newly formed Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes (later Yugoslavia).
layout: horizontal tricolor with coat of arms
symbols: The royal coat of arms — a crowned, mantled shield bearing a white double-headed eagle over a red field with a cross and four firesteels — centered on the flag.
disambiguation: Not to be confused with modern Serbia's flag, which uses the same red-blue-white tricolor with a differently detailed coat of arms.

context: Introduced by King Mongkut (Rama IV) as Siam opened to Western trade and diplomacy under the 1855 Bowring Treaty, replacing the plain red flag long used by Siamese ships with a distinguishing national emblem.
adopted: Introduced in 1855; replaced in 1916 by a red-white striped flag under Rama VI, itself replaced in 1917 by the modern red-white-blue Trairanga.
symbols: A white Chakri elephant (a sacred white elephant), standing in profile, centered on the red field.
disambiguation: Not to be confused with modern Thailand's five-band red-white-blue-white-red Trairanga, which carries no elephant emblem at all.

context: Introduced by the 13th Dalai Lama as part of a modernization program following Tibet's 1912 de facto independence from Qing China, adapting an older Tibetan military banner design into a state flag.
adopted: Introduced around 1912-1916 and used by the Tibetan government until the 1950-51 Chinese annexation; it continues in use today as the flag of the Tibetan government-in-exile.
layout: field with rays and central emblem
symbols: A yellow border; a snow-capped mountain in white at the base; a rising sun with alternating blue and red rays behind it; two snow lions holding a three-colored swirling jewel, with a further jewel below representing Tibetan sovereignty.
disambiguation: Not to be confused with any Chinese provincial or regional banner of the period; visually distinct due to its unique snow lion and rayed-sun motif.

context: Flown by the provincial administration of warlord Sheng Shicai, who ruled Xinjiang with heavy Soviet backing and patronage while nominally remaining a province of the Republic of China.
adopted: In use through Sheng's rule from the early-to-mid 1930s until his fall from power and Xinjiang's reversion to standard Republic of China administration in 1944.
symbols: A gold six-pointed star (hexagram) in the upper hoist area of the red field.
notes: A provincial/factional banner rather than a nationally recognized Republic of China flag.
disambiguation: Not to be confused with the Republic of China's Blue Sky White Sun flag that nominally still applied to the province, or Xinjiang's later, briefly-independent Second East Turkestan Republic flag, which uses a crescent and star rather than a hexagram.

context: Flown by the Yunnan Army/Yunnan Clique, the regional military faction that dominated Yunnan province through much of China's Warlord Era, tracing its prestige back to leading the 1915 National Protection War against Yuan Shikai's attempt to restore the monarchy.
adopted: In informal use as a factional/provincial banner through the Warlord Era into the late 1920s, fading out as the Nationalist government under Chiang Kai-shek consolidated control over Yunnan by 1930.
symbols: The single Chinese character "滇" (Diān, the classical name for Yunnan) in black, centered on the field.
notes: A provincial identifier banner rather than a flag issued by the central Republican government.
disambiguation: Not to be confused with any national Republic of China flag of the period; identifiable specifically by the Diān character, which names no other Chinese province.

context: Formed at the end of World War I by uniting the Kingdom of Serbia with former Austro-Hungarian South Slav territories under the Serbian Karadjordjevic dynasty, combining the Pan-Slavic colors already shared by Serbia, Croatia, and Slovenia's own flags.
adopted: Adopted in 1918 at the kingdom's founding as the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes (renamed Yugoslavia in 1929); superseded in 1941 by Axis occupation and partition following the German-led invasion.
disambiguation: Not to be confused with Russia's white-blue-red tricolor (different color order), Slovenia's or Slovakia's tricolors (same three colors with an added coat of arms), or the later Socialist Yugoslav flag, which adds a gold-bordered red star.

context: Adopted as a compromise between South Africa's British and Boer communities a generation after the Union's 1910 founding, incorporating the flags of the former Boer republics alongside the Union Jack to represent both heritages.
adopted: Adopted in 1928; it remained in use (latterly alongside the post-apartheid flag during the transition) until finally retired in 1994 with the end of apartheid and Nelson Mandela's inauguration.
symbols: Three small flags centered on the white band, all facing the hoist: the Union Jack, the Orange Free State flag, and the old South African Republic (Transvaal) flag.
disambiguation: Not to be confused with the modern South African flag adopted in 1994, which replaces this tricolor entirely with a six-color Y-shaped design.

context: This flag belongs to the Islamic Republic of Afghanistan, the internationally backed government formed after the 2001 fall of the first Taliban regime, which revived the black-red-green tricolor tradition used intermittently since the 1920s.
adopted: Formally adopted in 2004 with the new post-Taliban constitution; it replaced the plain white flag flown by the Taliban's earlier Islamic Emirate.
symbols: A circular gold-and-white national emblem sits centered on the red band, showing a mosque with a mihrab and pulpit flanked by wheat sheaves, with an inscribed banner below and rays above.
notes: This tricolor was Afghanistan's internationally recognized flag from 2004 to 2021 and is still used by opposition and diaspora groups who reject the current Taliban government.
disambiguation: Distinct from the plain white flag bearing a black Shahada inscription that the Taliban's Islamic Emirate has flown domestically since retaking the country in 2021.

context: Angola's flag dates from independence from Portugal in 1975, when the Marxist-oriented MPLA led the new government after a long armed liberation struggle.
adopted: Adopted on independence day, 11 November 1975, replacing Portuguese colonial rule.
symbols: A gold emblem centered across the boundary of the two bands combines a partial cog wheel with a crossed machete and hoe, topped by a five-pointed star, evoking industrial and agricultural labor.
disambiguation: Its labor-tool emblem invites comparison with Mozambique's flag, another former Portuguese colony whose flag also bears a crossed-tool emblem with a star, though Mozambique's field is a green-black-yellow tricolor rather than Angola's plain red-black bicolor.

context: The black double-headed eagle on red traces back to the 15th-century banner of national hero Skanderbeg, and has been revived in various forms across Albania's monarchy, kingdom, and communist periods.
adopted: The current plain version was readopted in 1992 after the fall of communism, when the red star placed above the eagle under the socialist government was removed.
symbols: A black double-headed eagle with outstretched wings fills the center of the red field.
disambiguation: Sometimes confused with Montenegro's flag, which also centers a double-headed eagle but adds a gold crown, scepter, and orb, plus a gold border around a deeper red field.

context: Andorra is a small co-principality historically ruled jointly by the Bishop of Urgell and the French head of state; its flag reflects both the French tricolor tradition and the country's own heraldic identity.
adopted: The blue-yellow-red tricolor came into use in the mid-19th century, with the coat of arms and its details fixed in law by the 1993 constitution.
symbols: The national coat of arms sits centered in the yellow band: a quartered shield bearing a mitre and crosier, oxen, three vertical red stripes, and two cows, under the Catalan motto 'Virtus Unita Fortior'.
disambiguation: Shares its blue-yellow-red vertical scheme with Chad and Romania, which use plain tricolors with no central emblem; Moldova is the closer match, since it also places a coat of arms in the center of an otherwise similar tricolor.

context: The flag was created when seven small Gulf emirates, formerly British-protected sheikhdoms known as the Trucial States, united into a single federation.
adopted: Adopted in 1971 upon the founding of the federation, drawing on the Pan-Arab colors associated with the early 20th-century Arab Revolt.
layout: horizontal triband with a vertical band at the hoist
disambiguation: Shares the Pan-Arab color palette with Kuwait's flag, but Kuwait places a black trapezoid at the hoist rather than the UAE's solid red rectangular band.

context: The light blue and white flag emerged during Argentina's war of independence from Spain, created by military and political leader Manuel Belgrano in 1812.
adopted: Declared the official national flag in 1816 by the Congress of Tucumán; the golden 'Sun of May' emblem, referencing the 1810 revolution against Spanish rule, was added to the flag a few years after its creation.
symbols: A golden sun with a human face and alternating straight and wavy rays is centered on the white band.
disambiguation: Neighboring Uruguay's flag uses the same Sun of May emblem, but places it in a white canton alongside alternating blue-and-white stripes rather than on a plain three-band field.

context: The tricolor revives the flag of the short-lived First Republic of Armenia (1918-1920), which was suppressed after Soviet annexation and re-emerged as Armenia moved toward independence from the USSR.
adopted: Readopted in 1990 as the Armenian SSR asserted sovereignty, and retained after full independence in 1991.
disambiguation: The unrecognized Republic of Artsakh (Nagorno-Karabakh) used a variant of this same tricolor with a white zigzag carpet-pattern chevron added at the fly.

context: Antarctica has no sovereign government and is governed instead by the Antarctic Treaty System, so it has never had an official national flag; this design, known as 'True South,' emerged from an open, crowd-sourced design process to give the continent a unifying unofficial symbol.
adopted: Introduced in 2018 and since adopted informally by some research stations, expeditions, and polar organizations, though it carries no legal or governmental status.
symbols: A white angular peak rises from the bottom half into the top half at the flag's center, evoking a compass needle pointing south, an iceberg, or a mountain, and its reflection.
notes: Unofficial design; no treaty body or government has formally adopted it as Antarctica's flag.
disambiguation: Predates and differs from an older, less widely used orange Antarctica flag design bearing a white map-and-laurel emblem reminiscent of the United Nations flag.

context: The flag was designed as Antigua and Barbuda gained self-government within the British West Indies, and was retained when the islands became fully independent.
adopted: Adopted in 1967 when the territory became an Associated State of the United Kingdom, and kept unchanged at full independence in 1981.
layout: triband with triangles and a sunburst
symbols: A rising golden sun with seven visible rays sits within the black band, symbolizing a new era; the black, blue, and white bands form a V-shape read as a bird taking flight, set within a broader red field.
disambiguation: Its red field and black-white color notes are sometimes mentally grouped with Trinidad and Tobago's flag, but Trinidad and Tobago uses a plain diagonal black band on red with no sunburst or triangular divisions.

context: The flag was designed shortly after the 1901 federation of Britain's Australian colonies into a single Commonwealth, combining imperial heritage with a distinctly southern-hemisphere star pattern.
adopted: Chosen through a public design competition in 1901, refined in 1908 with an extra point added to the Commonwealth Star, and given formal legal status by the Flags Act of 1953.
symbols: The Union Jack occupies the canton; below it a large seven-pointed white Commonwealth Star represents the federated states and territories; five white stars forming the Southern Cross constellation are scattered across the fly.
disambiguation: Closely resembles New Zealand's flag, which also places the Union Jack in the canton over a Southern Cross on blue, but New Zealand uses only four red-and-white stars and has no separate Commonwealth Star.

context: The red-white-red pattern is traditionally linked to a medieval legend about a Babenberg duke's blood-soaked tunic, and became the state's civil and national flag after the Habsburg monarchy collapsed at the end of World War I.
adopted: Formally adopted by the new Republic of Austria in 1918-1919, suppressed during the 1938-1945 Nazi annexation, and restored when the republic was reestablished in 1945.
disambiguation: Visually close to Latvia's flag, which also uses a red-white-red horizontal triband but with a narrower white band and a darker, more maroon shade of red.

context: The tricolor was first created in 1918 by the Azerbaijan Democratic Republic, a short-lived, Turkic, Muslim-majority parliamentary state, and was banned after Soviet annexation in 1920.
adopted: Restored as Azerbaijan moved toward independence from the Soviet Union around 1990-1991.
symbols: A white crescent moon and an eight-pointed star are centered on the red band.
disambiguation: Shares the crescent-and-star motif common to Turkey's flag, but Azerbaijan's star has eight points rather than five and sits on a light blue-red-green tricolor rather than a plain red field.

context: This version of the flag followed the 1966 abolition of the Burundian monarchy, adapting the tricolor-and-cross design used since independence from Belgian trusteeship in 1962.
adopted: Adopted in 1967 after the monarchy's fall, replacing the earlier flag's central royal drum emblem with three stars.
symbols: A white diagonal cross divides the field into red triangles (top and bottom) and green triangles (hoist and fly); a white central disc bears three red six-pointed stars outlined in green, arranged in a triangle.
disambiguation: The diagonal-cross layout resembles Jamaica's flag, which also divides its field into four triangles with a saltire, though Jamaica uses a gold cross on green and black rather than Burundi's white cross on red and green with a central star disc.

context: The flag emerged from the 1830 Belgian Revolution, in which the southern provinces of the United Kingdom of the Netherlands broke away to form an independent state.
adopted: Formally adopted in 1831, drawing its black, yellow, and red colors from the historic coat of arms of the Duchy of Brabant.
disambiguation: Uses the same three colors as Germany's flag, but Belgium arranges them as vertical bands in close-to-square proportions, while Germany's are horizontal bands on a wider rectangle.

context: The flag was designed shortly before independence from France as the territory then called Dahomey prepared for self-rule, using the green-yellow-red colors associated with Pan-Africanism.
adopted: First adopted in 1959 ahead of 1960 independence; replaced in 1975 by a plain green flag with a red star under the Marxist-Leninist government, then restored in 1990 when multi-party democracy returned and the country's name changed to Benin.
layout: vertical band with two horizontal bands
disambiguation: Shares its green-yellow-red Pan-African palette with Guinea's flag, but Guinea uses a plain vertical tricolor in red-yellow-green order rather than Benin's single hoist band paired with two stacked horizontal bands.

context: The flag was introduced after the 1983 revolution led by Thomas Sankara, when the country renamed itself from Upper Volta to Burkina Faso.
adopted: Adopted in 1984 in Pan-African colors, replacing the former black-white-red tricolor used since independence in 1960.
symbols: A five-pointed gold star sits centered across the boundary between the red and green bands.
disambiguation: Its horizontal red-and-green field with a central star recalls Ghana's flag, though Ghana adds a middle gold band and places a black rather than gold star at its center.

context: The flag was created during the 1971 Bangladesh Liberation War, as Bengali nationalists fought for independence from Pakistan.
adopted: First flown in 1971; the original wartime version included a yellow silhouette map of the country within the red disc, which was removed in 1972 to simplify the design after independence was secured.
layout: red field with disc and symbol
symbols: A red disc, offset slightly toward the hoist, sits on the green field, representing the rising sun and the sacrifice of those who died in the independence struggle.
disambiguation: Frequently compared to Japan's flag, since both feature a plain red disc on a solid field, but Bangladesh's disc sits on green and is shifted off-center, while Japan's is centered on white.

context: The Pan-Slavic white-green-red tricolor emerged as Bulgaria gained autonomy from the Ottoman Empire in the late 1870s.
adopted: First adopted around 1878; restored in its plain form in 1990 after the communist-era state emblem, added in 1946, was removed following the fall of the socialist government.
disambiguation: Easily confused with Hungary's flag, which uses the same three colors, but Hungary orders them red-white-green rather than Bulgaria's white-green-red.

context: Bahrain's red-and-white flag with a serrated edge is a long-standing regional Gulf design; the number of serrations has varied over the country's history.
adopted: The current five-point serrated pattern was fixed in 2002, when Bahrain's governing charter was revised and the monarchy restyled itself a kingdom.
layout: vertical bicolor with a serrated edge
symbols: Five white triangular points project from the white hoist band into the red field, conventionally read as representing the five pillars of Islam.
disambiguation: Shares its serrated-band concept with neighboring Qatar's flag, but Qatar's field is a dark maroon with nine serrations and a proportionally much wider white band.

context: The flag was designed for independence from the United Kingdom, chosen to reflect the islands' sea, sand, and sun rather than retaining British colonial symbols.
adopted: Adopted upon independence on 10 July 1973.
layout: horizontal triband with a hoist triangle
symbols: A black triangle points inward from the hoist edge, representing the unity and determination of the Bahamian people.
disambiguation: Its pale blue-toned bands loosely recall Botswana's flag, though Botswana's is a plain horizontal tricolor with a thin black-and-white band and no hoist triangle.

context: The flag was designed after the 1992-1995 Bosnian War, when the country's ethnically divided factions could not agree on a shared national symbol.
adopted: Imposed in 1998 by decision of the international High Representative overseeing the postwar peace settlement, intended to be neutral among the country's Bosniak, Serb, and Croat communities.
symbols: A yellow right triangle running from the top edge to the bottom edge near the hoist evokes the country's shape on the map; a row of white five-pointed stars, cut off at the top and bottom to suggest an endless sequence, runs along the triangle's diagonal edge.
disambiguation: Conceptually close to Kosovo's flag, another internationally designed postwar symbol pairing a blue field, a gold silhouette map of the country, and stars representing its communities.

context: This flag is a modified version of the flag used by the Byelorussian Soviet Socialist Republic, revived by referendum after independence rather than continuing with the white-red-white flag briefly used from 1991 to 1995.
adopted: Adopted following a 1995 referendum held under President Alexander Lukashenko, removing the Soviet-era hammer and sickle while keeping the red-and-green field and the decorative hoist pattern.
layout: horizontal bicolor with a decorative hoist band
symbols: A vertical red-on-white band of traditional Belarusian woven ornamentation runs along the hoist edge.
disambiguation: Nearly identical to the former Byelorussian SSR flag, differing mainly by the removal of the hammer, sickle, and red star that appeared on the Soviet-era version.

context: The flag developed from the banner of the pre-independence People's United Party, adapted for independence from the United Kingdom with an added second color as a gesture of political compromise.
adopted: Adopted upon independence in 1981, with red stripes added to the original blue-and-white party flag to represent the opposition party alongside the governing one.
symbols: A white disc at the center holds the national coat of arms: a shield with tools and a sailing ship, flanked by two woodcutters and topped by a mahogany tree, encircled by a wreath.
disambiguation: Its plain blue field with a white disc bearing a detailed coat of arms broadly resembles Fiji's flag layout, though Fiji retains a Union Jack canton and a shield-shaped, rather than circular, emblem.

context: Bolivia's tricolor traces back to the years just after independence from Spain in the 1820s, with the current color order fixed in the mid-19th century.
adopted: The red-yellow-green arrangement was fixed in 1851, building on flags used since the 1820s.
notes: This plain triband is the civil flag; Bolivia's state and war flags add the national coat of arms centered on the yellow band.
disambiguation: Uses the same red-yellow-green order as Ghana's flag, though Ghana adds a black five-pointed star centered on its yellow band.

context: The flag was introduced when Brazil's monarchy was overthrown and a republic proclaimed, replacing the earlier imperial flag while keeping its green-and-yellow color scheme.
adopted: Adopted on 19 November 1889, days after the republic's proclamation.
layout: green field with rhombus and central emblem
symbols: A yellow rhombus centered on the green field contains a blue celestial globe scattered with 27 white stars, one for each state and the federal district, arranged to mirror the sky over Rio de Janeiro at the moment of the republic's founding; a white banner curving across the globe reads 'ORDEM E PROGRESSO' (Order and Progress).
disambiguation: Its green field and yellow rhombus descend from the earlier flag of the Empire of Brazil (1822-1889), which used the same shapes but displayed the crowned imperial coat of arms instead of the current globe and motto banner.

context: The flag was designed for independence from the United Kingdom, chosen through a national competition to replace British colonial symbols.
adopted: Adopted upon independence on 30 November 1966.
symbols: A black trident head with a broken shaft is centered on the gold band, symbolizing a break from the full trident shown on the colonial-era badge, which itself referenced Britannia.
disambiguation: Its navy-and-gold vertical triband layout is fairly distinctive among Caribbean flags, most of which favor horizontal designs or more crowded emblems.

context: The flag reflects Brunei's status as a Malay Islamic sultanate, retained through its period as a British-protected state and into full independence.
adopted: Adopted in 1959 with Brunei's written constitution, and kept unchanged when the country achieved full independence in 1984.
symbols: A red national crest sits centered on the flag, combining a crescent moon, an umbrella-like royal parasol, wing-like flanking elements, and a banner inscribed with the state motto.
disambiguation: Unlike Malaysia's red-and-white striped flag with its blue Commonwealth-style canton, Brunei's flag is a plain diagonally striped field dominated entirely by its national crest rather than stars or stripes.

context: Bhutan calls itself Druk Yul, 'Land of the Thunder Dragon,' and its flag has featured the dragon in various forms since the mid-20th century, reflecting both Buddhist tradition and the monarchy.
adopted: In use in evolving versions since the mid-20th century, with its modern proportions and design fixed in 1969.
symbols: A large white dragon, coiled and facing the hoist, is centered across the diagonal boundary, clutching jewels in each of its four claws.
disambiguation: No other national flag depicts a dragon, making Bhutan's flag essentially unmistakable, though its plain diagonal split loosely echoes the diagonal band used on the Democratic Republic of the Congo's flag.

context: The flag was designed for independence from Britain, when the former Bechuanaland Protectorate became Botswana, deliberately avoiding the black-and-white racial imagery of apartheid-era South Africa in favor of a unifying stripe pattern.
adopted: Adopted upon independence on 30 September 1966.
layout: horizontal field with a bordered band
symbols: A black horizontal band, edged with thin white stripes, crosses the middle of the pale blue field, read as symbolizing racial harmony and water.
disambiguation: Its distinctive pale sky-blue field sets it apart from most neighboring countries' flags, in contrast to Somalia's flag, which uses a similarly light blue field but as a plain background for a single white star rather than a striped band.

context: Designed by independence leader Barthélemy Boganda ahead of self-government, the flag deliberately blends Pan-African colors with the French tricolor's red-white-blue, symbolizing unity between Africa and Europe.
adopted: Adopted in 1958 under self-government and retained after full independence from France in 1960.
layout: horizontal bands with a vertical stripe and canton star
symbols: A single vertical red band crosses all four horizontal bands at the center; a yellow five-pointed star sits in the upper hoist area of the blue band.
disambiguation: Distinguished from other multi-band African flags, such as Ethiopia's green-yellow-red horizontal tricolor with a central blue disc, by its added vertical red stripe crossing all bands and its star placed in the blue band rather than centered on the flag.

context: The maple leaf flag was adopted after a prolonged and contentious parliamentary debate under Prime Minister Lester Pearson's government, replacing designs that had retained the Union Jack.
adopted: Adopted on 15 February 1965, ending decades of use of the Canadian Red Ensign as the country's de facto flag.
symbols: A stylized red eleven-point maple leaf is centered in the wide white middle band.
notes: The red side bands are traditionally drawn narrower than the white center band (a 'Canadian pale' proportion), rather than three equal thirds.
disambiguation: Shares its red-white-red vertical triband layout with Peru's civil flag, which uses the same proportions but leaves the white center band plain rather than bearing a maple leaf.

context: The white cross on red descends from medieval military banners used by the Old Swiss Confederacy, later standardized as the modern federal state's official symbol.
adopted: Its square proportions and cross dimensions were fixed by federal decree in 1889, formalizing a design tradition going back centuries.
symbols: A white Greek cross, with arms of equal length that do not reach the flag's edges, is centered on the red square field.
notes: Switzerland's flag is square, one of very few national flags with that proportion.
disambiguation: The Red Cross humanitarian emblem is Switzerland's flag with its colors reversed (a red cross on white), chosen in honor of the movement's Swiss founder, Henry Dunant; the Vatican is the only other country using a square national flag.

context: The flag was adopted during Chile's war of independence from Spain, under the leadership of Bernardo O'Higgins.
adopted: Adopted in 1817, with its final proportions settled in later decades.
symbols: A blue square canton in the upper hoist corner holds a single white five-pointed star.
disambiguation: Frequently compared to the flag of the U.S. state of Texas, which independently uses a similar blue canton with a single white star set beside white and red bands.

context: The flag was created for the founding of the People's Republic in 1949, after the Chinese Communist Party's victory in the civil war.
adopted: Adopted just before the republic's formal proclamation on 1 October 1949.
symbols: A large yellow five-pointed star sits near the upper hoist corner, with four smaller yellow stars arced beside it, conventionally read as the Communist Party leading the unity of the country's social classes.
disambiguation: Vietnam's flag uses the same red field and yellow star motif, but shows only a single large centered star with no smaller accompanying stars.

context: The flag was adopted just before independence from France, using the orange-white-green tricolor to represent the country's northern savanna, the path to unity, and its southern forests.
adopted: Adopted in 1959, ahead of independence in 1960.
disambiguation: A well-known mirror image of Ireland's flag, which uses the same three colors in reverse order (green-white-orange).

context: Cameroon's flag evolved through its transition from French and British trust territories to a unified independent state; the current version with a central star marked the country's shift to a unitary form of government.
adopted: The striped tricolor was first used around independence and reunification in 1957-1961, with the star added in 1975 to mark the move to a unitary state.
symbols: A single yellow five-pointed star is centered on the red band.
disambiguation: Nearly identical to Senegal's flag, which uses the same three colors in the same order, but Senegal's star is green and sits on the central yellow band rather than the red band.

polity: the Democratic Republic of the Congo
context: This design revives the flag used from 1963 to 1971, before the Mobutu government renamed the country Zaire and adopted a different flag; it was restored as the country emerged from years of civil conflict.
adopted: Readopted in 2006 alongside a new constitution following the transition period after the Second Congo War.
symbols: A red diagonal stripe bordered in yellow runs from the lower hoist to the upper fly; a single yellow five-pointed star sits in the upper hoist corner.
disambiguation: Easily confused by name with the Republic of the Congo (its western neighbor, sharing the 'Congo' name), but the two flags are visually distinct: this one is sky blue with a diagonal red-and-yellow stripe and a star, while the Republic of the Congo's is a plain green-yellow-red diagonal tricolor.

context: This flag was originally used from independence in 1959 until 1970, then set aside during the country's Marxist-Leninist one-party period, before being restored as multi-party rule returned.
adopted: Readopted in 1991 after a national conference ended one-party communist rule, replacing the red flag with a crossed hoe and hammer used since 1970.
disambiguation: Easily confused by name with the neighboring Democratic Republic of the Congo, but the flags are visually distinct: this one is a plain green-yellow-red diagonal tricolor, while its neighbor's is sky blue with a diagonal red-and-yellow stripe and a star.

context: Colombia's tricolor descends from the flag used by Gran Colombia, the short-lived early-19th-century state that also included what are now Venezuela, Ecuador, and Panama.
adopted: The specific double-width yellow band and 2:1:1 proportions were fixed by decree in 1861.
notes: This plain triband is the civil flag; Colombia's state flag adds the national coat of arms centered on the flag.
disambiguation: Shares its yellow-blue-red palette and origin with Ecuador and Venezuela, both also descended from the Gran Colombia flag; Ecuador adds a central coat of arms and Venezuela adds a row of stars, while Colombia's civil flag remains plain.

context: The flag represents the Union of the Comoros, an archipelago nation with a Muslim-majority population, and was updated as part of a new constitution establishing a federal structure for its islands.
adopted: Adopted around 2001-2002 with the new constitution creating the Union of the Comoros.
layout: green field with canton triangle and horizontal stripes
symbols: A green triangle at the hoist holds a white crescent moon and four white five-pointed stars stacked vertically; four horizontal stripes (yellow, white, red, and blue) fill the rest of the field, each stripe and star representing one of the archipelago's four main islands.
notes: One of the four islands the flag references, Mayotte, remains a French territory and does not use this flag; it flies the French tricolor instead.
disambiguation: Shares the crescent-and-star Islamic imagery of Mauritania's flag, though Mauritania's is a plain green field with a single gold crescent and star rather than Comoros' striped field with a hoist triangle and four stars.

context: The flag was introduced as Cabo Verde moved from a one-party state, which had shared a common flag design with Guinea-Bissau since their joint 1975 independence from Portugal, to multi-party democracy.
adopted: Adopted in 1992, replacing the earlier red-yellow-green flag inherited from the shared liberation movement era.
layout: blue field with a striped band and circle of stars
symbols: A band of narrow white-red-white stripes crosses the lower third of the blue field; a circle of ten yellow five-pointed stars is centered above the band, one for each of the archipelago's main islands.
disambiguation: Its blue field and circle of stars invite comparison with the European Union's flag, which similarly places a ring of gold stars on blue, though the EU's circle holds twelve fixed stars and no striped band.

context: The original blue-and-white flag, inherited from the earlier Central American Federation, was modified when President Jose Maria Castro Madriz added a red stripe inspired by the French tricolor.
adopted: The red stripe was added in 1848; this plain version, without the national coat of arms, is the civil flag.
notes: This plain five-band version is the civil flag; the state flag adds the national coat of arms within a white disc on the red band.
disambiguation: Both use a thick central band flanked by thinner outer stripes, but Thailand's flag reverses the color scheme and meaning, running red-white-blue-white-red rather than Costa Rica's blue-white-red-white-blue.

context: The flag was designed in 1849 by Cuban exiles and sympathizers seeking independence from Spain, and became the flag of the new republic after Spanish and then U.S. military rule ended.
adopted: First flown around 1850 and adopted as the official national flag on 20 May 1902, when the Republic of Cuba was established.
symbols: A red equilateral triangle at the hoist contains a single white five-pointed star, set against five alternating blue-and-white horizontal stripes.
disambiguation: Puerto Rico's flag was deliberately designed in solidarity with Cuba's independence movement using the same layout with colors swapped: a blue triangle and star against red-and-white stripes, rather than Cuba's red triangle against blue-and-white stripes.

context: The flag was created for Cyprus's independence from Britain, deliberately avoiding the blue-and-white of Greece and the red of Turkey to remain neutral between the island's Greek and Turkish communities.
adopted: Adopted upon independence on 16 August 1960.
symbols: A copper-orange silhouette map of the island of Cyprus is centered on the white field, with two crossed olive branches beneath it symbolizing peace between its communities.
disambiguation: One of only a few national flags to depict the country's own outline; Kosovo's flag is another rare example, though it places a gold map on blue with stars rather than Cyprus's copper map on white with olive branches.

context: The flag was originally created for Czechoslovakia in 1920; a blue triangle was added at the hoist specifically to distinguish it from Poland's flag, which used the same plain white-over-red bicolor.
adopted: Adopted for Czechoslovakia in 1920 and retained by the Czech Republic after the country's peaceful split from Slovakia in 1993, despite earlier debate over whether continued use was appropriate once Czechoslovakia ceased to exist.
symbols: A blue triangular wedge extends from the hoist edge partway across the white and red bands.
disambiguation: Its blue hoist triangle over a white-and-red field is visually close to the Philippines' flag, though the Philippines adds a sun-and-three-stars emblem within the triangle and inverts the whole flag in wartime.

context: The black-red-gold combination traces to the volunteer Lutzow Free Corps of the Napoleonic Wars and the liberal, unification-minded revolutionaries of 1848; it was first used as a national flag under the Weimar Republic after World War I.
adopted: Readopted by West Germany in 1949 and by the reunified Germany in 1990, continuing the tradition begun in 1919 and interrupted by the Nazi period's swastika flag.
disambiguation: Shares its three colors with Belgium's flag, but Germany arranges them as horizontal bands on a wide rectangle rather than Belgium's vertical bands on near-square proportions.

context: The flag was designed for independence from France, its two colors representing the country's two main communities, the Issa Somali and the Afar.
adopted: Adopted upon independence on 27 June 1977.
symbols: A white triangle at the hoist holds a single red five-pointed star, set against a field divided diagonally into light blue (top) and green (bottom).
disambiguation: Shares its light blue color and single-star symbolism with neighboring Somalia's flag, though Somalia's is a plain light blue field with a centered white star and no green band or hoist triangle.

context: The flag was designed for independence from Britain, chosen to depict the endangered Sisserou parrot found only on Dominica.
adopted: Adopted upon independence on 3 November 1978.
symbols: A cross made of three colored bands (yellow, black, and white) divides the green field into quarters; a red circle at the center, ringed by ten green five-pointed stars representing the island's ten parishes, contains a purple Sisserou parrot.
disambiguation: The only national flag to depict a full-color parrot, making it essentially unmistakable among world flags despite its cross-and-field layout echoing a few other Caribbean designs.

context: According to a long-standing national legend, the flag fell from the sky during a 13th-century battle in what is now Estonia, and it is often cited as one of the oldest continuously used flag designs in the world, though its exact origins are uncertain and no single legislative adoption date exists.
adopted: Traditionally dated to 1219; its use by the state and civilians was regulated by various decrees in later centuries rather than a single founding law.
symbols: A white Nordic cross, its vertical bar shifted toward the hoist, sits on the plain red field.
disambiguation: The simplest of the Nordic cross flags: unlike Norway's flag, which adds a blue cross outlined in white on the same red field, Denmark's uses only the two colors red and white.

context: The flag was adopted when the Dominican Republic broke away from Haitian rule over the eastern part of the island of Hispaniola, led by the independence movement known as the Trinitarios.
adopted: Adopted in February 1844, when independence from Haiti was declared.
symbols: A white cross divides the field into four quarters of alternating blue and red; the national coat of arms, a shield with an open Bible and a small cross flanked by a national flag on either side, sits centered where the cross bars meet, beneath a ribbon bearing the national motto.
notes: The version shown here, bearing the coat of arms, is the state flag; a plain version without the coat of arms is used informally by private citizens.
disambiguation: Its neighbor on the same island, Haiti, shares the blue-and-red color pair but uses horizontal bands with a different coat of arms rather than the Dominican Republic's white cross and quartered field.

context: The design was used by the FLN (National Liberation Front) during the Algerian War of Independence against France in the 1950s and carried directly into statehood.
adopted: Became the national flag at independence from France in July 1962, replacing French colonial rule.
symbols: A red crescent, opening toward the fly, straddling the boundary between the green and white panels.
A single red five-pointed star centered inside the crescent's opening.
disambiguation: Unlike Turkey's or Pakistan's flags, which place a white crescent and star on a single-color field, Algeria's crescent and star are red and sit astride a green-and-white split field.

context: The tricolor descends from the flag flown by Gran Colombia, the short-lived republic uniting Venezuela, Colombia, Ecuador, and Panama after independence from Spain in the 1820s.
adopted: The state flag bearing the national coat of arms was formalized around 1900, building on the yellow-blue-red tricolor used since Ecuador separated from Gran Colombia in 1830.
symbols: The national coat of arms centered on the flag: an Andean condor with wings spread atop an oval shield.
Within the shield, snow-capped Mount Chimborazo, the Guayas River with a steamship, and a sun with zodiac signs.
The shield is bordered by four small national flags and framed below by a laurel and palm wreath.
notes: The plain tricolor without the coat of arms is used as a civil/merchant ensign; the version with arms is the state and national flag.
disambiguation: Colombia and Venezuela fly nearly identical yellow-blue-red tricolors from the same Gran Colombia heritage; Ecuador is distinguished by always displaying its condor-and-Chimborazo coat of arms at center.

context: The red-white-black tricolor descends from the Arab Liberation Flag adopted after the 1952 revolution that ended the monarchy, and was later shared in modified forms by other Arab republics.
adopted: The current version with the Eagle of Saladin was adopted in 1984, continuing a tricolor tradition used with different central emblems since the 1950s-70s union periods.
symbols: A golden eagle (the Eagle of Saladin) centered on the white band, wings spread, facing the hoist.
The eagle grasps a scroll bearing the country's name in Arabic script.
disambiguation: Syria, Iraq, and Yemen share the same red-white-black tricolor lineage; Egypt is distinguished by its golden Eagle of Saladin, versus Syria's two green stars or Iraq's green Kufic script.

context: Eritrea won independence from Ethiopia after a decades-long armed struggle led by the Eritrean People's Liberation Front (EPLF), formalized by a 1993 referendum.
adopted: Formally adopted in the mid-1990s, reworking the EPLF's wartime banner and the wreath emblem from Eritrea's earlier UN-federated 1952 flag into a new design.
symbols: A red triangle extending from the hoist toward the fly, flanked by a green triangle above and a blue triangle below.
A gold olive wreath encircling an upward-growing olive branch, centered on the red triangle.
disambiguation: The olive-branch-and-wreath emblem echoes Eritrea's 1952 UN-era flag (a plain light-blue field with the same wreath), but the current flag replaces that field with the red-green-blue triangle design from the independence struggle.

context: The basic red-yellow-red proportions were introduced in the 18th century as a naval ensign meant to be easily distinguished at sea, and were carried forward through the country's various 19th and 20th century regime changes.
adopted: The current constitutional flag, with the national coat of arms on the yellow band, was formally confirmed after Spain's transition to democracy and the 1978 constitution; only the design of the coat of arms has changed under different governments.
notes: The plain triband without the coat of arms is the merchant/civil ensign used mainly at sea; the state and national flag normally displayed on land carries the coat of arms offset toward the hoist on the yellow band.
disambiguation: Portugal's neighboring flag uses green and red rather than red and yellow; among red-yellow-red tribands, Spain's plain civil version (shown here) is easily confused with its own state flag, which adds the coat of arms.

context: The blue-black-white tricolor originated as the banner of an Estonian student fraternity in the 1880s during a period of national cultural awakening under Russian imperial rule.
adopted: Adopted as the national flag when Estonia first declared independence in 1918, banned during the Soviet occupation from 1940, and restored as Estonia regained independence around 1990-1991.
disambiguation: The blue-black-white combination is distinctive worldwide, with no widely confused look-alike among current national flags.

context: Ethiopia's green-yellow-red horizontal stripes are the historical origin of the modern Pan-African color scheme, having been used in various forms since the late 19th and early 20th centuries.
adopted: The current flag, with a central emblem added after the fall of the Derg military government, was adopted in the mid-1990s under Ethiopia's federal constitution and had its proportions refined further in 2009.
notes: The plain tricolor without any central emblem has been used at various points in Ethiopia's flag history, including periods before the current national emblem was introduced.
disambiguation: Ghana, Guinea, Mali, and Senegal all use the same green-yellow-red palette in Pan-African tribute to Ethiopia; Ethiopia's own current flag is normally distinguished by a blue disc bearing a yellow star at its center, which is absent from this image.

context: Finland declared independence from Russia in December 1917 amid the collapse of the Russian Empire, and quickly moved to establish its own national symbols distinct from its former ruler.
adopted: Adopted in 1918 in the aftermath of independence, replacing the flags used under Russian rule.
disambiguation: Sweden's flag uses the same Nordic cross layout but in blue and yellow; Finland is distinguished by its blue-on-white color scheme.

context: Fiji became independent from British colonial rule in 1970 and chose to retain British-derived flag elements from its colonial-era ensign rather than break entirely with the past.
adopted: Adopted at independence in 1970, based on the earlier colonial ensign; proposals to remove the Union Jack in the 2010s were ultimately not carried out.
symbols: The Union Jack occupies the canton at the upper hoist.

The Fijian shield, taken from the colonial coat of arms, sits off-center toward the fly: it shows a red cross on white, a British lion holding a cocoa pod, and quarters with sugar cane, a coconut palm, bananas, and a white dove.
disambiguation: Tuvalu also flies a light-blue field with a Union Jack canton; Fiji is distinguished by its detailed shield emblem at the fly, versus Tuvalu's ring of stars.

context: The tricolor emerged from the French Revolution, combining the traditional colors of Paris (blue and red) with the white of the monarchy as a symbol of national unity.
adopted: Formally adopted by the revolutionary government in the 1790s, and has remained the national flag through France's later republics, empires, and restorations, apart from a brief reversion to the white royal flag.
disambiguation: Italy's flag uses the same vertical tricolor layout with green instead of blue; France is distinguished by its blue-white-red order and cooler hues.

context: Micronesia's four island states (Chuuk, Kosrae, Pohnpei, and Yap) had been administered together as part of the US-run Pacific Islands Trust Territory before moving toward self-government.
adopted: Adopted in 1978 as the federation was being organized, using the blue of the earlier UN trusteeship flag as a nod to that transitional period.
symbols: Four white five-pointed stars arranged in a diamond pattern at the center, one for each of the four constituent states.
disambiguation: Palau's flag also uses a plain blue field but bears a single large gold disc rather than stars; Micronesia is distinguished by its four-star diamond arrangement.

context: Gabon gained independence from France in 1960 as part of the wider decolonization of French Equatorial Africa.
adopted: Adopted at independence in 1960, replacing the flag used during French colonial administration.
disambiguation: The color choice and horizontal layout is broadly shared with several African tricolors, but Gabon's specific green-yellow-blue combination (forest, equatorial sun, Atlantic Ocean) is not duplicated by any neighboring state.

context: The design layers the cross of St George (England and Wales), the saltire of St Andrew (Scotland), and the saltire of St Patrick (Ireland), reflecting the political union of these kingdoms.
adopted: The current version was adopted in 1801 when the Kingdom of Great Britain and the Kingdom of Ireland merged into the United Kingdom, adding St Patrick's cross to the 1606 union flag of England and Scotland.
symbols: A red cross edged in white (St George's cross) laid over the whole field.
A white saltire on blue in the background (St Andrew's cross), visible in the diagonal quarters.
A narrower red saltire offset within the white one (St Patrick's cross), interleaved with St Andrew's saltire.
disambiguation: Several former British territories and Commonwealth countries (e.g. Fiji, Australia) place the Union Jack as a canton within a larger flag; the UK's own flag is the union design alone, without an added field or additional emblem.

context: The five-cross design revives medieval Georgian heraldic banners and was promoted by opposition and church figures in the years before it returned to official use.
adopted: Formally readopted as the national flag in 2004 following the Rose Revolution, replacing the maroon-and-black tricolor used since Georgia's post-Soviet independence in the early 1990s.
symbols: A large red St George's cross spanning the full width and height of the white field.
Four smaller red Bolnisi crosses (a stylized cross with flared arms), one in each of the four white quarters.
disambiguation: England's flag is a plain St George's cross on white with no additional small crosses; Georgia is distinguished by the four Bolnisi crosses filling its quarters.

context: Ghana became the first sub-Saharan African country to gain independence from European colonial rule in the postwar era, and its flag was designed as a deliberate Pan-African symbol for other African independence movements to follow.
adopted: Adopted at independence in 1957, drawing its colors from Ethiopia's flag as a tribute to Africa's oldest independent state; the black star was added as a symbol of African freedom, referencing Marcus Garvey's Black Star Line.
symbols: A single black five-pointed star centered on the yellow band.
notes: A different flag with a black star on an eagle emblem was used briefly in the mid-1960s before this design was restored.
disambiguation: Several African tricolors share the same red-yellow-green palette; Ghana is distinguished by its solid black star centered on the yellow band, without any additional emblem.

context: Guinea was the first French West African colony to vote for full independence rather than continued association with France, in a 1958 referendum.
adopted: Adopted at independence in 1958, using Pan-African colors arranged vertically in the style of the French tricolor Guinea had just broken from.
disambiguation: Mali's flag uses the same three colors in a vertical tricolor but in the reverse order (green-yellow-red), making the two flags mirror images of one another.

context: The Gambia is a narrow country following the course of the Gambia River, which shaped the choice of a blue central stripe representing the river running through the land.
adopted: Adopted at independence from Britain in 1965.
notes: Narrow white fimbriations separate the main red, blue, and green bands.
disambiguation: The specific red-blue-green combination with white edging is not closely duplicated by any neighboring country's flag.

context: The flag was first used by the PAIGC independence movement during its armed struggle against Portuguese colonial rule and was carried into statehood after independence was declared.
adopted: Adopted when independence was unilaterally declared in 1973 (internationally recognized in 1974), based on Pan-African colors shared with the PAIGC's sister movement in Cape Verde.
symbols: A single black five-pointed star centered on the red hoist band.
disambiguation: Cape Verde used a nearly identical flag from 1975 until changing its own design in 1992; Guinea-Bissau has kept the original PAIGC-derived pattern.

context: Equatorial Guinea is made up of a mainland region and several islands, a geography reflected in both the flag's blue triangle (representing the sea link between them) and the six stars of its coat of arms.
adopted: Adopted at independence from Spain in 1968.
symbols: A blue triangle extending from the hoist edge, representing the sea between the mainland and island territories.
The national coat of arms centered on the white band: a grey silk-cotton tree above a scroll reading the national motto "Unidad, Paz, Justicia" (Unity, Peace, Justice).
Six small yellow six-pointed stars arc above the shield, representing the mainland and five main islands.
disambiguation: The hoist-side triangle recalls flags such as Guyana's or the Philippines', but Equatorial Guinea is set apart by its green-white-red horizontal bands and silk-cotton-tree coat of arms.

context: The blue-and-white cross design originated among Greek revolutionaries fighting for independence from Ottoman rule in the 1820s, with the colors representing the sky and sea and the cross representing Orthodox Christianity.
adopted: The nine-stripe version shown here was made the single official civil and state flag in 1978, unifying earlier separate civil and naval flag traditions.
symbols: A white cross on a blue square canton at the upper hoist.
Nine alternating horizontal blue and white stripes filling the rest of the field.
notes: The nine stripes are popularly said to represent the syllables of the independence-era motto "Eleftheria i Thanatos" (Freedom or Death).
disambiguation: The canton-plus-stripes structure loosely recalls flags like the United States', but Greece is immediately distinguished by its blue-and-white coloring and cross-in-canton rather than stars.

context: Grenada is nicknamed the "Isle of Spice" for its nutmeg production, which is reflected directly in the flag's imagery.
adopted: Adopted at independence from Britain in 1974.
symbols: A red border frames the flag, bearing seven yellow five-pointed stars: three along the top edge, three along the bottom edge, and one inside a red disc at the center of the flag.
The main field is divided into yellow triangles (top and bottom) and green triangles (hoist and fly).
A stylized gold nutmeg pod sits inside the green triangle at the hoist.
notes: The seven stars represent Grenada's seven parishes.
disambiguation: The combination of a red border, yellow/green triangles, and a nutmeg emblem is unique to Grenada among national flags.

context: Greenland is a self-governing territory within the Kingdom of Denmark; its flag was chosen through a public design competition held as the territory expanded its home rule.
adopted: Adopted in 1985 following the design competition, intended to visually distinguish Greenland from Denmark's own cross flag while remaining part of the kingdom.
symbols: A large circle offset toward the hoist, its upper half red and its lower half white, straddling the boundary between the flag's white top and red bottom halves.
disambiguation: Unlike Japan's flag, which places a single solid red disc on an all-white field, Greenland's disc is itself split red-over-white and sits on a field that is also divided white-over-red.

context: Guatemala's blue-and-white colors descend from the flag of the United Provinces of Central America, the federation that briefly united several Central American states after independence from Spain.
adopted: The blue-white-blue tricolor was adopted in 1871; the national coat of arms at its center was substantially updated in 1968.
symbols: The national coat of arms centered on the white band: a resplendent quetzal bird perched atop a scroll.
The scroll reads the date of Central American independence, framed by a wreath, with crossed rifles and swords behind it.
disambiguation: El Salvador, Honduras, and Nicaragua all use the same light-blue-white-light-blue triband from their shared federation history; Guatemala is distinguished by its quetzal-bearing coat of arms.

context: Guyana is the only English-speaking country on the South American mainland, having gained independence from Britain in the 1960s.
adopted: Adopted at independence in 1966.
symbols: A red triangle extending from the hoist, outlined in black.
A gold triangular arrowhead nested inside the red triangle, outlined in white, both set against the green field.
disambiguation: The nested double-triangle "arrowhead" design is unique to Guyana among national flags.

context: Like its neighbors, Honduras's flag descends from the banner of the United Provinces of Central America, and its stars reflect an enduring aspiration toward Central American reunification.
adopted: Adopted in 1866, based on the earlier federal flag.
symbols: Five blue five-pointed stars arranged in an X-shaped pattern across the white central band.
disambiguation: El Salvador, Guatemala, and Nicaragua also use blue-white-blue tribands from the same federation heritage; Honduras is distinguished by its five stars arranged in an X, representing the five original federated states.

context: Croatia adopted its modern flag amid multi-party elections and rising nationalist sentiment as Yugoslavia began to break apart, ahead of its formal declaration of independence in 1991.
adopted: Adopted in 1990, combining the traditional pan-Slavic red-white-blue tricolor with Croatia's historic checkerboard coat of arms.
symbols: The Croatian coat of arms centered at the top of the flag: a red-and-white checkerboard shield (the "šahovnica").
A crown above the shield made up of five smaller historical shields representing Croatia's regions.
disambiguation: Russia, Slovakia, Serbia, and Slovenia all use variations of the same red-white-blue tricolor; Croatia is distinguished by its checkerboard coat of arms placed at the top center of the flag.

context: Haiti's revolutionary leaders are said to have created the blue-and-red flag by tearing the white band out of the French tricolor during the Haitian Revolution, symbolically rejecting French colonial rule.
adopted: The state flag bearing the coat of arms was adopted in 1806, building on the blue-and-red design first used around Haiti's 1803-04 independence from France.
symbols: A white central panel bearing the national coat of arms: a palm tree topped with a Phrygian cap of liberty.
The palm tree stands over a green hillock and is flanked by national flags and stacked weapons.
A scroll below reads the national motto "L'Union Fait La Force" (Unity Makes Strength).
notes: A plain blue-over-red bicolor without the coat of arms is used as the civil flag.
disambiguation: Liechtenstein also uses blue and red as its main colors but in a completely different layout; Haiti's state flag is distinguished by its white central panel and palm-tree coat of arms.

context: The tricolor's colors trace back to Hungary's medieval royal coat of arms, and the flag became a rallying symbol during the 1848 revolution against Habsburg rule.
adopted: The plain tricolor without any state emblem was reinstated in 1957 after the 1956 uprising, removing the communist coat of arms that had been added in 1949.
disambiguation: Bulgaria's flag uses the same three colors in white-green-red order; Hungary is distinguished by its red-white-green order and by carrying no central emblem.

context: The red-and-white banner is said to trace back to the flag of the medieval Majapahit Empire, and was revived as a nationalist symbol in the early 20th century under Dutch colonial rule.
adopted: Adopted in 1945 when independence from the Netherlands was proclaimed.
disambiguation: Indonesia's flag is famously nearly identical to Monaco's, differing officially only in exact proportions; the two are frequently cited as the closest look-alike pair among national flags.

context: The tricolor was adapted from the Swaraj flag used by the Indian National Congress in the independence movement against British rule.
adopted: Adopted in 1947 as India became independent, with the spinning-wheel emblem of the earlier Congress flag replaced by the Ashoka Chakra.
symbols: A navy-blue 24-spoke wheel (the Ashoka Chakra) centered on the white band, taken from the ancient Ashoka Pillar.
disambiguation: Ireland and Niger use similarly ordered saffron/orange-white-green tricolors, but India is distinguished by its central navy Ashoka Chakra wheel.

context: The tricolor was associated with the Young Ireland movement of the mid-19th century and was intended to symbolize hoped-for peace between Ireland's Gaelic Catholic and Protestant unionist traditions.
adopted: Given formal constitutional status as the national flag in 1937, after earlier use during the 1916 Easter Rising and the subsequent Irish Free State period.
disambiguation: Ivory Coast uses nearly the same three colors in reverse order (orange-white-green), making the two flags a well-known mirror-image pair.

context: The current flag was introduced after the 1979 Islamic Revolution overthrew the Pahlavi monarchy, replacing the old imperial lion-and-sun emblem with religious script and a new central symbol.
adopted: Adopted in 1980, keeping the pre-existing green-white-red tricolor but changing the central emblem and adding repeated religious script along the stripe edges.
symbols: A stylized red emblem at the center of the white band, formed from a rendering of the word "Allah" that also suggests a tulip shape.
The phrase "Allahu Akbar" (God is Great) repeated in white Kufic script along the inner edges of the green and red bands.
