disambiguation: Iran's own pre-1979 flag used the same green-white-red tricolor but with a lion-and-sun emblem instead of the current calligraphic symbol and script border.

context: Iraq's tricolor belongs to the same Arab Liberation Flag family adopted after the 1958 revolution that overthrew the monarchy, shared with Egypt, Syria, and Yemen.
adopted: The current simplified version, with the religious script rendered in a plain green Kufic script, was adopted in 2008, removing three green stars that had been added to an earlier version of the design.
symbols: The phrase "Allahu Akbar" (God is Great) written in green Kufic script, centered on the white band.
disambiguation: Egypt, Syria, and Yemen share the same red-white-black Arab Liberation Flag colors; Iraq is distinguished by its green Kufic script reading "Allahu Akbar" across the white band.

context: Iceland's flag colors are said to represent the country's landscape: blue for the sea and mountains, white for snow and ice, and red for volcanic fire.
adopted: Used from 1915 as a home-rule ensign under Danish sovereignty and formally adopted as the national flag when Iceland became a fully independent republic in 1944.
disambiguation: Norway's flag uses the identical blue-field, white-fimbriated red Nordic cross design; the two are distinguished mainly by their differing proportions.

context: The design was based on the flag of the Zionist movement, itself modeled on the traditional Jewish prayer shawl (tallit), which is white with blue stripes.
adopted: Adopted in 1948 upon the declaration of the State of Israel.
symbols: Two horizontal blue stripes near the top and bottom edges of the white field.
A blue six-pointed Star of David (Magen David) centered on the flag.
disambiguation: Israel's flag is unique among national flags for its Star of David emblem and tallit-derived stripe pattern.

context: The tricolor tradition dates back to Napoleonic-era Italian republics of the 1790s and was carried forward through Italian unification in the 19th century.
adopted: The current plain tricolor was adopted in 1946 when Italy became a republic, removing the House of Savoy's coat of arms that had appeared on the flag of the Kingdom of Italy.
disambiguation: Mexico uses a nearly identical green-white-red vertical tricolor but adds a central coat of arms; Italy's flag is plain with no emblem.

context: Jamaica's flag was chosen ahead of independence from Britain, with a design intentionally avoiding red, white, and blue to distinguish it from British and neighboring colonial-era flags.
adopted: Adopted at independence in 1962.
symbols: A diagonal gold saltire crossing the flag from corner to corner, dividing the field into four triangles.
notes: The green triangles sit at top and bottom, and the black triangles at hoist and fly.
disambiguation: Jamaica is one of the few national flags to contain no red, white, or blue, and its plain gold saltire on green-and-black is not closely duplicated elsewhere.

context: The flag is based on the Arab Revolt Flag raised during the 1916 uprising against Ottoman rule, and was adapted for use by the Emirate of Transjordan under British administration.
adopted: Adopted in 1928 and retained after Jordan's full independence in 1946, with a seven-pointed star added to the Arab Revolt design.
symbols: A red triangle extending from the hoist across the black, white, and green horizontal bands.
A white seven-pointed star centered on the red triangle, representing the seven verses of the Quran's opening sura and/or Arab unity.
disambiguation: The flag of Palestine is nearly identical but lacks Jordan's white seven-pointed star on the red triangle.

context: The red sun disc has been associated with Japan for centuries, tied to the country's traditional self-description as the "Land of the Rising Sun."
adopted: Formally established as the national flag by law in 1999, codifying a design that had already been in de facto use for generations.
symbols: A red disc centered on the white field, representing the sun.
disambiguation: Bangladesh (green field with a red disc) and Palau (blue field with a gold disc) use a similar single-disc-on-field concept, but Japan's white-and-red combination is not duplicated by any other national flag.

context: Kazakhstan adopted its own national symbols after gaining independence from the Soviet Union in 1991, drawing on Turkic and steppe cultural imagery.
adopted: Adopted in 1992, replacing the Kazakh Soviet Socialist Republic's flag.
symbols: A golden sun with radiating rays at the center of the field.
A golden steppe eagle (berkut) soaring beneath the sun.
A vertical strip of traditional Kazakh ornamental patterning running along the hoist edge.
disambiguation: Several former Soviet Central Asian states use light-blue accents, but Kazakhstan is the only one with a solid cyan field paired with a sun-and-eagle emblem.

context: The flag was based on the banner of the Kenya African National Union (KANU), the party that led the country to independence from Britain.
adopted: Adopted at independence in 1963.
symbols: A traditional red, white, and black Maasai shield centered on the flag.
Two white spears crossed behind the shield.
notes: Narrow white fimbriations separate the black, red, and green bands.
disambiguation: The shield-and-spears emblem is distinctive to Kenya; while its tricolor palette is broadly similar to other African flags, no other country combines it with a Maasai shield.

context: Kyrgyzstan adopted new national symbols after gaining independence from the Soviet Union, drawing on the folk epic of Manas and traditional nomadic yurt imagery.
adopted: Adopted in 1992, replacing the Kyrgyz Soviet Socialist Republic's flag.
symbols: A yellow sun with 40 rays centered on the red field, the number said to represent 40 legendary Kyrgyz tribes.
A stylized tunduk, the wooden crown of a traditional yurt roof, depicted inside the sun.
disambiguation: Kazakhstan's flag also centers a golden sun emblem, but on a light-blue field with an eagle rather than Kyrgyzstan's red field and tunduk pattern.

context: The Angkor Wat silhouette had appeared on Cambodian flags before the Khmer Rouge and communist periods, and was revived after the monarchy was restored following the early-1990s Paris Peace Accords.
adopted: Readopted in 1993 as Cambodia's constitutional monarchy was reestablished.
symbols: A white silhouette of the Angkor Wat temple, with its three towers, centered on the wide red band.
disambiguation: The Angkor Wat temple silhouette is unique to Cambodia among national flags, making it easily distinguished from other blue-red triband designs.

context: The design was based on a coat of arms granted to the former Gilbert Islands colony in the 1930s, carried into independence from Britain.
adopted: Adopted at independence in 1979.
symbols: A yellow frigatebird in flight over a yellow rising sun on the upper red half of the flag.
Alternating blue and white wavy horizontal stripes filling the lower half, representing the Pacific Ocean.
disambiguation: Sun-and-bird motifs appear on several Pacific island flags, but Kiribati's wavy blue-and-white ocean stripes across the lower half are distinctive.

context: The flag was designed for the newly independent two-island federation, with symbolism referencing both the shared history of its people and the union of the two islands.
adopted: Adopted at independence from Britain in 1983.
symbols: A black diagonal band, edged in yellow, running from the lower hoist to the upper fly.
Two white five-pointed stars placed side by side on the black band.
A green triangle fills the upper hoist corner and a red triangle fills the lower fly corner.
disambiguation: The diagonal-band layout invites loose comparison to Tanzania's flag, but Saint Kitts and Nevis is distinguished by its two white stars set on the black diagonal band.

context: The design builds on a flag first used in the late Joseon dynasty of the 1880s, combining traditional Korean cosmological symbolism with a modern national banner.
adopted: Adopted in 1948 with the founding of the Republic of Korea.
symbols: A red-and-blue Taegeuk (yin-yang) circle centered on the white field, representing cosmic balance.
Four black trigrams from the I Ching, one in each corner, representing heaven, earth, fire, and water.
disambiguation: South Korea's flag is the only national flag to feature I Ching trigrams, making it unmistakable among world flags.

context: The flag draws on the Arab Revolt Flag color tradition shared across several Arab states, adopted as Kuwait moved to full independence from British protection.
adopted: Adopted at independence from Britain in 1961.
symbols: A black trapezoid running along the hoist edge, cutting across the green, white, and red horizontal bands.
disambiguation: Jordan, Palestine, and the UAE share the same black-white-green-red palette; Kuwait is distinguished by its black hoist-side trapezoid rather than a triangle or separate vertical band.

context: The flag was introduced when the communist Pathet Lao movement established the Lao People's Democratic Republic, replacing the flag of the former Kingdom of Laos.
adopted: Adopted in 1975 with the founding of the Lao People's Democratic Republic.
symbols: A white disc centered on the wide blue band, representing the full moon over the Mekong River and the unity of the Lao people.
disambiguation: Cambodia's flag shares a similar red-and-blue palette, but Laos is distinguished by its plain white disc rather than a temple silhouette.

context: The cedar tree is a millennia-old symbol of Lebanon, referenced in ancient texts, and was placed on the flag as the country moved toward independence from French mandatory rule.
adopted: Adopted in 1943 as Lebanon gained independence from the French Mandate.
symbols: A green cedar tree centered on the wide white band.
disambiguation: Austria's flag uses the same red-white-red triband proportions, but Lebanon is immediately distinguished by its central green cedar tree.

context: Liberia was founded in the early 19th century as a settlement for freed and freeborn African-Americans organized by the American Colonization Society, and it declared independence as Africa's first modern republic in 1847.
adopted: Adopted in 1847 at independence, deliberately modeled on the flag of the United States to reflect the settlers' origins.
layout: horizontal field of stripes with canton
symbols: Eleven alternating red and white horizontal stripes, said to represent the signers of Liberia's 1847 Declaration of Independence.
A single white five-pointed star centered on a blue canton in the upper hoist corner, representing Liberia's status as the sole independent black republic in Africa at the time.
disambiguation: Closely modeled on the flag of the United States, from which it is distinguished mainly by its single star rather than fifty and its eleven rather than thirteen stripes.

context: This tricolor was originally the flag of the Kingdom of Libya from independence in 1951 until the 1969 coup that brought Muammar Gaddafi to power; opposition forces revived it during the 2011 civil war as a symbol of rejecting Gaddafi's rule.
adopted: Readopted in 2011 by the National Transitional Council during the uprising against Gaddafi and confirmed as the national flag after his fall, replacing the plain green flag used from 1977 to 2011.
symbols: A white crescent moon opening toward the hoist with a white five-pointed star in its opening, both centered on the black middle stripe.
disambiguation: Not to be confused with the plain green flag used under Gaddafi from 1977 to 2011, which this tricolor replaced and which carried no other markings at all.

context: Designed as Saint Lucia moved toward self-government within the West Indies Associated States in the late 1960s, and retained when the island gained full independence from Britain in 1979.
adopted: Adopted in 1967 and carried over at independence in 1979; the shade of blue was lightened in a minor 2002 revision.
symbols: A black triangle edged in white, representing the island's twin volcanic peaks the Pitons, overlaid by a smaller gold triangle representing sunshine, both centered on a light blue field standing for sea and sky.
disambiguation: Not to be confused with the Bahamas' flag, which uses a similar aquamarine-and-gold palette but arranges it as horizontal bands with a black hoist triangle rather than Saint Lucia's stacked twin-peak triangle.

context: Liechtenstein's blue-and-red flag dates to its 1921 constitution, but the two colors alone proved indistinguishable from Haiti's flag when both delegations arrived at the 1936 Berlin Olympics under near-identical banners.
adopted: The gold princely crown was added in 1937 to the existing blue-over-red bicolor to give the principality a flag distinct from Haiti's.
symbols: A gold princely crown, representing the ruling House of Liechtenstein, placed in the upper hoist area of the blue band.
disambiguation: Distinguished from Haiti's plain blue-over-red bicolor — the flag it was mistaken for at the 1936 Olympics — solely by the added gold crown.

context: Sri Lanka (then Ceylon) adopted a lion flag based on the historic banner of the Kandyan Kingdom upon gaining independence from Britain in 1948; vertical stripes representing the island's minority communities were added when it became a republic in 1972.
adopted: The core lion design was adopted in 1951, with the saffron and green minority stripes added in 1972 when Ceylon became the Republic of Sri Lanka.
layout: plain field with charge and border stripes
symbols: A dark green vertical stripe at the hoist edge, representing Sri Lankan Muslims, followed by a saffron/orange stripe representing Tamils, then the larger maroon panel bearing the lion device.
A gold lion passant holding a kastane sword, representing the Sinhalese people, facing the hoist within the maroon panel.
Four gold bo-tree leaves, one in each corner of the maroon panel, representing Buddhism.
disambiguation: One of the few national flags centered on a large heraldic animal rather than stripes or geometric emblems; unlike Bhutan's dragon flag, its animal is confined to one panel alongside separate community-representing stripes.

context: Adopted to mark the fortieth anniversary of independence from Britain, replacing an earlier post-independence flag design that had carried a shield, spear, and knobkerrie evoking the country's warrior history.
adopted: Adopted in 2006, replacing the 1987 flag (itself a revision of the original 1966 independence flag) as part of a deliberate shift toward symbols of peace.
symbols: A black mokorotlo, the traditional conical straw Basotho hat, outlined in white and centered on the white middle stripe.
disambiguation: The pale blue field recalls Botswana's flag, but Lesotho's is a plain horizontal triband with a central hat emblem rather than Botswana's black-and-white striped band.

context: First adopted after Lithuania declared independence from Russia at the end of World War I, the tricolor was suppressed during decades of Soviet annexation and revived as Lithuania moved toward restoring its independence in the late 1980s.
adopted: Originally adopted in 1918; formally readopted in 1988-1990 as Lithuania reasserted sovereignty from the Soviet Union.
disambiguation: Not to be confused with Bolivia's flag, which uses the same three colors in reverse order (red over yellow over green) as a triband rather than Lithuania's yellow-green-red sequence.

context: The red-white-blue tricolor derives from the colors of the Grand Duchy's coat of arms, which came into wider civilian use in the 19th century following Luxembourg's involvement in the 1830 Belgian Revolution period.
adopted: In informal use through the 19th and early 20th centuries, it was formally established by law as the national flag in 1972.
disambiguation: Nearly identical to the Netherlands' flag, differing only in its lighter, brighter shade of blue and its more elongated proportions.

context: The dark red-and-white pattern is tied to a medieval legend of a wounded Latvian chieftain wrapped in a white sheet that stained red at the edges, and it was adopted as the national flag when Latvia first became independent after World War I.
adopted: Adopted in 1918 at independence, suppressed under Soviet rule, and formally restored in 1990 as Latvia regained independence.
disambiguation: Distinguished from Austria's red-white-red flag by its much narrower white stripe (roughly one-fifth the width of each red band, not an equal third) and its distinctive dark, brownish-red shade.

context: The plain red field was the traditional color of the Alaouite dynasty; a green pentagram was added in 1915 while Morocco was under French and Spanish protectorate administration, and the flag was retained after full independence in 1956.
adopted: The green star was added to the historic red field in 1915; the flag continued unchanged after independence from France and Spain in 1956.
symbols: A green five-pointed star (the Seal of Solomon) centered on the red field.
disambiguation: The pre-protectorate Sultanate flag used before 1915 was a plain red field with no star at all; this modern flag adds the green pentagram that distinguishes it.

context: The red and white colors are the heraldic colors of the House of Grimaldi, the princely family that has ruled Monaco since the Middle Ages.
adopted: Formally established as the national flag in 1881, based on the long-standing Grimaldi dynastic colors.
disambiguation: Nearly identical to Indonesia's flag (also red over white), differing only in its more elongated proportions; it is the reverse of Poland's white-over-red flag.

context: Adopted as Moldova asserted sovereignty from the Soviet Union in 1990, the tricolor echoes the blue-yellow-red flag long used by neighboring Romania, reflecting the two countries' shared Romanian linguistic and cultural heritage.
adopted: Adopted in 1990, ahead of full independence in 1991, with the state coat of arms added to the center.
layout: vertical tricolor with coat of arms
symbols: The Moldovan coat of arms centered on the yellow band: a golden eagle holding a cross in its beak and clutching an olive branch and scepter, with a shield bearing an aurochs head on its chest.
disambiguation: Effectively Romania's blue-yellow-red tricolor with the addition of Moldova's central coat of arms; without that emblem the two flags are indistinguishable, and both also share their color scheme with Chad's flag.

context: Adopted ahead of independence from France, combining white (a color linked to purity and to the historic Merina monarchy) with the red and green long associated with the island's earlier kingdoms.
adopted: Adopted in 1958 as Madagascar became a self-governing republic within the French Community, two years before full independence in 1960.
disambiguation: Not to be confused with Bangladesh's flag, which also pairs red and green but as a green field with a plain red disc rather than Madagascar's solid tricolor blocks.

context: The flag builds on a much older plain red sultanate flag, with a green rectangle and Islamic crescent added in the early 20th century to affirm the country's Muslim identity; the current form was fixed around independence from British protection.
adopted: Finalized in essentially its current form in 1965 at independence, refining earlier 20th-century sultanate flags.
symbols: A white crescent moon centered on a green rectangle, itself centered on a red field; the crescent represents Islam and the green rectangle represents progress and prosperity.
disambiguation: Shares the crescent-on-green motif with Mauritania's flag, but Maldives sets its green field as a bordered inner rectangle on solid red rather than Mauritania's full-width green field with a five-pointed star alongside the crescent.

context: The green-white-red tricolor dates to the 1821 Army of the Three Guarantees at the end of Mexico's war of independence from Spain; the central eagle-on-cactus emblem, drawn from the Aztec founding legend of Tenochtitlan, has appeared in various forms ever since.
adopted: The tricolor dates to 1821; the current precise eagle design and proportions were standardized by law in 1968.
layout: vertical tricolor with coat of arms
symbols: The national coat of arms centered on the white band: a golden eagle perched on a prickly pear cactus, devouring a rattlesnake, commemorating the Aztec legend that marked the founding site of Tenochtitlan.
disambiguation: Shares Italy's green-white-red vertical tricolor exactly, but is distinguished by the detailed eagle-and-cactus coat of arms centered on the white band, which Italy's plain tricolor lacks.

context: Adopted as the islands moved toward self-government under a Compact of Free Association with the United States, ending decades as part of the US-administered Pacific Islands Trust Territory.
adopted: Adopted in 1979 upon becoming self-governing, and retained when full independence took effect in 1986.
symbols: Two diagonal stripes, orange above white, running from the lower hoist to the upper fly and widening as they go, said to represent the Ratak and Ralik island chains and rising confidence.
A white 24-pointed star in the upper hoist corner, its four longer rays representing the four main population centers and its points together representing the 24 municipal districts.
disambiguation: The single diagonal stripe and star-on-blue arrangement recalls the Solomon Islands' flag, but the Marshall Islands uses two stripes (orange and white) rather than one thin yellow stripe, and places a single large star rather than the Solomon Islands' five small stars.

context: Adopted as part of a diplomatic settlement with Greece, which had objected to the original 1992 independence-era flag's use of the ancient Vergina Sun symbol as a claimed Greek historical emblem.
adopted: Adopted in 1995 under the interim accord with Greece, replacing the 1992 flag that had featured the Vergina Sun.
symbols: A golden sun with eight broadening rays radiating from a central disc, filling the red field.
notes: The 1992-1995 predecessor flag, withdrawn under the 1995 accord, used the more historically pointed Vergina Sun rather than this simplified broadening-ray sun.
disambiguation: Shares a golden-sun-on-colored-field concept with Kazakhstan's blue flag, but North Macedonia's sun has broad triangular rays reaching the flag's edges on a red field, unlike Kazakhstan's circular sun with thin rays and an eagle beneath it.

context: First flown for the short-lived Mali Federation with Senegal in 1959 with a human figure (kanaga) centered on the yellow stripe, the figure was dropped when Mali became fully independent alone in 1960-1961.
adopted: The plain tricolor was adopted in 1961 after Mali left the Mali Federation, removing the earlier kanaga figure from the 1959 federation flag.
disambiguation: The exact mirror image of Guinea's flag, which uses the same three colors in reverse order (red, yellow, green from the hoist).

context: The red-and-white colors are traditionally linked to medieval Norman rule of Malta; the George Cross was added to commemorate the collective military decoration awarded to the Maltese people by King George VI in 1942 for their endurance under wartime siege.
adopted: Adopted in 1964 at independence from Britain, incorporating the George Cross awarded in 1942.
symbols: The George Cross, outlined in red, displayed in the upper hoist corner of the white band.
disambiguation: Shares Poland's red-and-white palette, but Malta's bands run vertically rather than horizontally and carry the George Cross emblem that Poland's plain bicolor lacks.

context: Adopted as part of a broader constitutional transition under the ruling military government, replacing a socialist-era flag that had carried a blue canton with a cogwheel and rice-stalk emblem.
adopted: Adopted in 2010, replacing the flag used since Myanmar's 1974 socialist constitution.
symbols: A large white five-pointed star centered across all three stripes.
disambiguation: Echoes the three-stripes-plus-star concept of Ghana's flag, but reverses the color order (yellow-green-red rather than red-gold-green) and uses a large white star spanning all three bands rather than a small black star on the center stripe alone.

context: Readopted as Montenegro moved toward separating from its union with Serbia, reviving the red-and-gold royal colors and double-headed eagle associated with the pre-1918 Montenegrin kingdom.
adopted: Adopted in 2004 while still part of the State Union of Serbia and Montenegro, and retained after full independence in 2006.
layout: plain field with border and coat of arms
symbols: A golden double-headed eagle, crowned and holding a scepter and orb, centered on the red field.
A shield on the eagle's chest bearing a golden lion passant on a green ground.
A gold border framing the entire flag.
disambiguation: Not to be confused with Albania's simpler red flag bearing a plain black double-headed eagle; Montenegro adds a gold border, royal crown, and shield-bearing coat of arms that Albania's flag omits.

context: The red-blue-red triband with the ancient Soyombo emblem dates to the 1940s under the socialist Mongolian People's Republic; the communist star that had topped the Soyombo symbol was removed as Mongolia transitioned away from one-party rule.
adopted: The Soyombo-bearing tricolor was formalized around 1940; the red star atop the Soyombo was dropped in 1992 following Mongolia's democratic transition.
symbols: The golden Soyombo emblem, a stack of traditional symbols including fire, sun, moon, and yin-yang elements, centered on the hoist-side red band.
A blue center band representing the eternal sky, flanked by red bands representing progress and prosperity.
disambiguation: Structurally similar to Andorra's blue-yellow-red vertical triband with a central emblem, but Mongolia places its emblem on the hoist-side band of a red-blue-red sequence rather than centered on a middle band.

context: Refined from the flag flown at independence from Portugal in 1975, the design keeps the red hoist triangle and star of the ruling FRELIMO movement's banner while adding the crossed rifle, hoe, and open book emblem.
adopted: The current emblem arrangement was fixed in 1983, building on the original 1975 independence-era flag.
symbols: A red triangle at the hoist bearing a yellow five-pointed star, within which sit a crossed AK-47 rifle and hoe over an open book, representing defense, agriculture, and education.
disambiguation: Shares Kenya's black-red-green tricolor-plus-emblem concept, but Mozambique arranges the colors as a green-black-yellow triband with a hoist triangle, and is the only national flag in the world to depict a modern firearm.

context: The green field with gold crescent and star was adopted ahead of independence from France to affirm Mauritania's Islamic identity; red stripes were added decades later following a 2017 constitutional referendum, said to represent the sacrifices of those who resisted colonization and slavery.
adopted: The green-and-gold crescent flag was adopted in 1959, ahead of independence in 1960; red stripes were added at the top and bottom in 2017.
layout: horizontal border with crescent and star
symbols: A gold crescent moon opening upward with a gold five-pointed star above it, both centered on the green field.
disambiguation: Shares a green-field star-and-crescent design with the Maldives and Comoros, but Mauritania is distinguished by its thin red top-and-bottom stripes, added in 2017, framing the green field.

context: Adopted at independence from Britain, its four horizontal bands are unique among national flags and were chosen to represent the island's diverse population and landscape.
adopted: Adopted in 1968 at independence from Britain.
disambiguation: Its red-yellow-green palette recalls widely used Pan-African colors as in Ghana's or Ethiopia's flags, but Mauritius adds a distinct blue band and arranges all four as plain horizontal stripes rather than a tricolor with a star or emblem.

context: Adopted at independence from Britain, the rising sun on the black stripe symbolized the dawn of freedom for Malawi and for Africa as a whole.
adopted: Adopted in 1964 at independence; briefly replaced in 2010 by a version with a full white sun and reordered stripes, before the original 1964 design was restored in 2012.
symbols: A red rising sun with 31 triangular rays, centered on the black top stripe.
notes: A 2010 redesign replaced the black stripe's rising red sun with a full white sun centered on the flag and reordered the stripes; this proved unpopular and the original 1964 version shown here was reinstated in 2012.
disambiguation: Uses the same black-red-green sequence as Kenya's flag, but Malawi replaces Kenya's central shield-and-spears emblem with a rising sun on the black stripe alone.

context: Adapted from the flag of the earlier Federation of Malaya at independence, the design was updated when Malaya, Singapore, Sabah, and Sarawak merged to form Malaysia in 1963; the fourteen stripes and star points originally counted Singapore among the constituent states.
adopted: Adopted in 1963 at Malaysia's formation, revising Malaya's 1950 eleven-stripe flag; the fourteen stripes and points were kept even after Singapore's departure in 1965.
layout: horizontal field of stripes with canton
symbols: Fourteen alternating red and white horizontal stripes, representing the 13 states and the federal government.
A gold crescent moon and 14-point star on a blue canton in the upper hoist corner, also representing the 13 states plus the federal government.
notes: The fourteen stripes and star points originally represented Singapore as a constituent state; after Singapore's 1965 separation the count was retained to represent the federal government alongside the 13 remaining states.
disambiguation: Modeled closely on the Stars and Stripes of the United States, differing in its lower stripe count, its crescent-and-star canton in place of stars, and its blue-yellow color scheme in the canton.

context: Adopted at independence from South African administration, combining colors associated with the main independence movement, SWAPO, with symbolism of the sun, sky, land, and water.
adopted: Adopted in 1990 at independence.
symbols: A gold sun with twelve triangular rays in the upper hoist blue triangle, representing life and energy.
A red diagonal band edged in white running from the lower hoist to the upper fly, dividing the blue upper-hoist triangle from the green lower-fly triangle.
disambiguation: Structurally similar to Tanzania's diagonally divided flag, but Namibia uses a red band edged in white (rather than Tanzania's black band edged in yellow) and adds a golden sun to its upper triangle, which Tanzania's flag lacks.

context: Adopted ahead of independence from France, the orange stripe evokes the Sahara desert in the country's north, the green stripe the fertile Sudanian region in the south, and the white stripe hope and purity.
adopted: Adopted in 1959, a year before independence in 1960.
symbols: A solid orange disc, representing the sun, centered on the white middle stripe.
disambiguation: Uses the same saffron-white-green tricolor as India's flag, differing mainly in that Niger's central emblem is a plain solid disc rather than India's spoked Ashoka Chakra wheel.

context: Selected through a national design competition ahead of independence from Britain, with green representing the country's agriculture and natural wealth and white representing peace and unity.
adopted: Adopted in 1960 at independence, based on the winning entry from a public design competition.
disambiguation: Not to be confused with Ireland's flag, which similarly places a white band beside a green one but pairs it with orange on the far side rather than Nigeria's mirrored green-white-green.

context: Derived from the blue-white-blue flag of the 19th-century United Provinces of Central America, of which Nicaragua was once a member, reflecting shared regional identity among the Central American republics.
adopted: Adopted in its modern form in 1908 and reaffirmed in 1971.
layout: horizontal triband with coat of arms
symbols: The national coat of arms centered on the white band: a triangle enclosing five volcanoes beneath a rainbow and a Phrygian cap, ringed by text reading "REPUBLICA DE NICARAGUA" and "AMERICA CENTRAL".
disambiguation: Nearly identical to El Salvador's flag, which shares the same blue-white-blue triband and Central American Federation heritage; the two are distinguished mainly by the specific details of their central coats of arms.

context: Evolved from the orange-white-blue Prince's Flag flown during the 16th-century Dutch Revolt against Spanish rule, with red gradually displacing orange in general use by the 17th century, reportedly for greater visibility at sea.
adopted: In de facto use for centuries, the red-white-blue tricolor was formally confirmed as the national flag by royal decree in 1937.
disambiguation: Nearly identical to Luxembourg's flag, differing mainly by Luxembourg's lighter, brighter shade of blue and more elongated proportions.

context: Adopted after Norway's 1814 constitution ended centuries of union with Denmark and began a new union with Sweden, the design layers Norway's own blue cross onto the red-and-white cross long used by Denmark to assert a distinct national identity.
adopted: Adopted in 1821, combining Denmark's traditional red-and-white cross with blue to mark Norway's separate identity within its union with Sweden.
symbols: A blue cross outlined in white, offset toward the hoist, on a red field.
disambiguation: Shares its exact three colors with Iceland's flag, but reverses their emphasis — Norway is a red field with a blue-on-white cross, while Iceland is a blue field with a red-on-white cross.

context: The double-pennant shape descends from royal and Hindu banner traditions used for centuries in Nepal; the moon and sun symbols were simplified into their current geometric forms under the 1962 constitution.
adopted: The overall design has roots going back generations, with the moon and sun symbols standardized into their current plain form by the 1962 constitution.
symbols: A white crescent moon with trailing rays in the upper pennant.
A white twelve-rayed sun in the lower pennant.
disambiguation: Nepal's flag is the world's only non-rectangular national flag, so unlike other entries here it has no close look-alike among the rectangular national flags of other countries.

context: Adopted at independence from a joint Australian, British, and New Zealand administered UN trusteeship, its design encodes Nauru's small size and equatorial location in the Pacific.
adopted: Adopted in 1968 at independence.
layout: plain field with stripe and star
symbols: A narrow gold horizontal stripe crossing the blue field, representing the equator.
A white twelve-pointed star below the stripe, positioned to show Nauru's location just south of the equator, its points representing the twelve original tribes of Nauru.
disambiguation: Shares a blue-field-with-star Pacific design language with the Marshall Islands' flag (also in this catalog), but Nauru uses a single plain gold equator stripe rather than the Marshall Islands' two diagonal orange-and-white stripes.

context: Developed from colonial-era maritime ensigns flown from 1869, the flag was formally adopted as New Zealand's national flag in the early 20th century, retaining the Union Jack to reflect ties to Britain.
adopted: Adopted as the national flag in 1902, building on earlier colonial ensign use.
layout: plain field with canton and stars
symbols: The Union Jack in the canton, marking historical ties to Britain.
Four red five-pointed stars edged in white on the fly, representing the Southern Cross constellation.
disambiguation: Nearly identical to Australia's flag, which shares the same blue field, Union Jack canton, and Southern Cross theme; Australia adds a large seven-pointed Commonwealth Star and six white stars in the constellation, versus New Zealand's four plain red stars.

context: Adopted after Sultan Qaboos bin Said took power in a 1970 palace coup and began modernizing the country, replacing the plain red flag used under his predecessor Said bin Taimur.
adopted: Adopted in 1970, with the design further refined in 1995.
layout: horizontal triband with hoist band and emblem
symbols: The national emblem — a khanjar dagger in its sheath crossed over two swords — in white on the red vertical band at the hoist.
disambiguation: Shares a red-white-green-plus-hoist-band structure with the United Arab Emirates' flag, but Oman arranges white, red, and green as horizontal stripes with the red hoist band bearing the khanjar emblem, while the UAE uses a vertical green-white-black triband with a plain, unmarked red hoist band.

context: Based on the flag of the All-India Muslim League, adopted at independence and partition from British India in 1947; the dark green and crescent-and-star represent Islam and the Muslim majority, while the white stripe represents religious minorities.
adopted: Adopted in 1947 at independence.
layout: plain field with hoist stripe and charge
symbols: A white vertical stripe at the hoist, representing religious minorities.
A white crescent moon and five-pointed star centered on the green field, representing progress and light.
disambiguation: Shares the green-white-and-crescent theme with Algeria's flag, but Pakistan uses a solid dark green field with a white hoist stripe, while Algeria splits its field into equal green and white vertical halves with the crescent and star centered across both.

context: Adopted at independence from Colombia in 1903, with the blue and red quarters said to represent the country's two main political parties of the era, the Conservatives and Liberals, united in the white quarters symbolizing peace.
adopted: Adopted in 1903, traditionally credited to members of the Amador family, at Panama's separation from Colombia.
symbols: A blue five-pointed star in the white upper-hoist quarter.
A red five-pointed star in the white lower-fly quarter.
disambiguation: Shares a blue-white-red palette and single-star motif with Chile's flag, though Chile arranges its colors as a horizontal bicolor with a blue star-bearing canton rather than Panama's four quartered blocks with two separate stars.

context: Descended from an earlier horizontal red-white-red flag introduced during the independence campaign led by José de San Martín in the early 1820s, later reoriented into vertical stripes.
adopted: The vertical red-white-red arrangement was adopted in 1825, refining the horizontal design used since the early 1820s independence campaign.
notes: This plain version is the civil flag; Peru's state and war flags add the national coat of arms centered on the white band, which the plain civil flag shown here omits.
disambiguation: Easily confused with Canada's red-white-red vertical triband; unlike Canada's maple leaf, Peru's plain civil flag carries no central emblem at all (that is reserved for the separate state flag).

context: First flown when Filipino revolutionaries declared independence from Spain in 1898, having been sewn by exiles in Hong Kong; the flag can be flown inverted, red stripe uppermost, to signal a state of war.
adopted: Adopted in 1898 at the declaration of independence; the officially specified shade of blue was restored to a lighter royal blue in a 1998 centennial law after decades of a darker navy blue under prior administrations.
symbols: A white equilateral triangle at the hoist, representing equality.
A golden sun with eight rays centered in the triangle, representing the eight provinces that first rose against Spanish rule.
A small gold five-pointed star at each corner of the triangle, representing the three main island groups: Luzon, Visayas, and Mindanao.
notes: The flag is flown with the blue stripe uppermost in peacetime and inverted, red stripe uppermost, to signal a state of war.
disambiguation: Structurally similar to Cuba's flag, which also pairs a hoist triangle with horizontal stripes, but the Philippines uses a white triangle with a sun-and-stars emblem over blue-and-red stripes, while Cuba uses a red triangle with a single star over blue-and-white stripes.

context: Adopted as Palau moved toward self-government ahead of full independence from the US-administered Trust Territory of the Pacific Islands, the golden disc represents the full moon, traditionally considered the ideal time for harvest, fishing, and important cultural activities.
adopted: Adopted in 1981 as Palau became self-governing, and retained at full independence in 1994.
symbols: A golden disc, representing the full moon, positioned slightly toward the hoist on the light blue field.
disambiguation: Compositionally very close to Bangladesh's flag, which likewise places a single colored disc off-center toward the hoist on a plain field, differing only in Palau's sky-blue field and gold disc versus Bangladesh's green field and red disc.

context: Adopted ahead of independence from Australian administration, chosen through a national design competition won by a teenage student.
adopted: Adopted in 1971, four years before independence in 1975, based on the winning entry in a national design contest.
symbols: A gold silhouette of a raggiana bird-of-paradise, a bird native to the country, on the red lower-fly triangle.
Five white stars representing the Southern Cross constellation on the black upper-hoist triangle.
disambiguation: Shares the Southern Cross motif seen on Australia's, New Zealand's, and Samoa's flags, but Papua New Guinea is unique in placing the stars on a black diagonal triangle alongside a bird-of-paradise rather than on a plain blue field.

context: The white and red derive from the white eagle on a red shield in Poland's coat of arms; the flag was formally established after Poland regained its independence at the end of World War I, having been partitioned among neighboring empires for over a century.
adopted: Formally adopted in 1919, after Poland regained independence in 1918.
notes: A state variant adds the crowned white eagle coat of arms to the white stripe for official use, while the plain bicolor shown here is the civil flag.
disambiguation: The exact reverse of Monaco's and Indonesia's red-over-white flags, distinguished simply by having white on top rather than red.

context: Adopted at the founding of the Democratic People's Republic of Korea, deliberately replacing the white Taegukgi flag associated with the Korean Empire and pre-division Korean identity, which the South retained.
adopted: Adopted in 1948 at the country's founding, marking a symbolic break from the shared Taegukgi tradition.
layout: horizontal bands with disc and star
symbols: A red five-pointed star within a white circle, positioned toward the hoist on the wide red center band, representing revolutionary tradition.
disambiguation: The clearest disambiguation is with South Korea's flag: the two Koreas' flags share no design elements, as North Korea replaced the white field and red-and-blue taegeuk symbol still used by South Korea with this blue-red-blue band-and-star design.

context: Adopted after the 1910 revolution that overthrew the Portuguese monarchy and established a republic, replacing the old blue-and-white royal flag with green and red, colors often associated with hope and with those who died in the revolutionary struggle.
adopted: Adopted in 1911, following the republican revolution of 1910.
layout: vertical bicolor with coat of arms
symbols: The national coat of arms centered on the dividing line: an armillary sphere, symbolizing the Age of Discoveries, behind a shield bearing five small blue shields arranged in a cross and a red border with castles.
disambiguation: Unlike many green-and-red national flags such as Bangladesh's or Mexico's, Portugal is a plain two-color bicolor of unequal-width bands rather than a tricolor, carrying a far more heraldically detailed coat of arms.

context: The red-white-blue tricolor tradition dates to the early 19th century, following Paraguay's break from Spanish colonial rule, and Paraguay is one of the very few countries whose flag differs between its front and back.
adopted: The tricolor dates to 1842, with the current standardized design and proportions set by later 20th and early 21st century legislation.
symbols: The national seal, a yellow star within a circle bearing the words "REPUBLICA DEL PARAGUAY", centered on the white band on the obverse side shown here.
notes: Paraguay's flag is one of the few in the world with different designs on each side: the front (obverse) bears the national star seal shown here, while the back (reverse) bears a different Treasury seal with a lion and liberty cap.
disambiguation: Shares the common red-white-blue horizontal tricolor of the Netherlands, Luxembourg, and Russia, but is distinguished by its central national seal and its unique two-sided design, which those plain tricolors lack.

context: Based on the Pan-Arab colors of the 1916 Arab Revolt flag, this design was adopted by the Palestine Liberation Organization in the 1960s and has been used as the flag of the State of Palestine since its 1988 declaration.
adopted: Adopted by the Palestine Liberation Organization in 1964, and used as the flag of the State of Palestine following its 1988 declaration.
symbols: A red triangle at the hoist, spanning the full height of the flag.
disambiguation: Nearly identical to Jordan's flag, which uses the same black-white-green bands and red hoist triangle drawn from the same Arab Revolt origin; Jordan's version adds a white seven-pointed star on the red triangle that Palestine's flag lacks.

context: Developed from earlier plain red flags used by Gulf sheikhdoms in the 19th century, the maroon shade and serrated white band were adopted to distinguish Qatar's flag from neighboring Bahrain's similar red-and-white design.
adopted: Adopted in its current maroon-and-white serrated form in 1949.
layout: plain field with serrated hoist band
symbols: A white band with nine serrated points along its edge, running the length of the hoist side.
notes: Qatar's flag is notably elongated compared to most national flags, with an official length-to-height ratio of roughly 2.75 to 1.
disambiguation: Closely related to Bahrain's flag, which uses the same serrated-band-at-hoist design; Qatar is distinguished by its darker maroon (rather than Bahrain's brighter red) field, its nine serrations versus Bahrain's five, and its much more elongated proportions.

context: The blue-yellow-red tricolor traces back to the mid-19th century union of the Danubian principalities of Wallachia and Moldavia; the communist-era state emblem that had been added to the flag's center was removed after the 1989 revolution that overthrew Nicolae Ceaușescu.
adopted: The plain tricolor was restored in 1989 following the revolution, removing the socialist coat of arms that had been added to the flag's yellow band in 1948.
disambiguation: Famously nearly identical to Chad's flag, which uses the same blue-yellow-red vertical tricolor; Romania's flag is also shared in color scheme, though not emblem, with Moldova's flag, which adds a central coat of arms that Romania's plain version lacks.

context: After the dissolution of the Soviet Union, Russia restored the pre-revolutionary imperial-era tricolor as a symbol of continuity with pre-Soviet statehood and a break from communist symbolism.
adopted: Readopted in 1991 as the Russian Federation emerged from the Soviet collapse, restoring the flag last used before the 1917 revolution; formally confirmed by law in 1993.
disambiguation: Identical in design to the pre-1917 imperial Russian tricolor already catalogued for that earlier era; distinct from Slovenia's or Slovakia's tricolors, which add a coat of arms to a similar white-blue-red base, and from the Netherlands' flag, which reverses the order to red-white-blue.

context: Adopted after the 1994 genocide and civil war, as part of a broader effort to build a new national identity centered on unity and reconciliation rather than the divisions of the past.
adopted: Adopted in 2001, replacing the red-yellow-green flag with a black "R" that had been in use since Rwanda's 1962 independence.
symbols: A golden sun with radiating rays, positioned in the upper fly area of the blue band, symbolizing enlightenment and unity.
disambiguation: Not to be confused with the pre-2001 Rwandan flag (red-yellow-green with a black "R"), which this design entirely replaced to distance the state from the genocide era.

context: The modern kingdom's flag continues the plain shahada banners flown by the Al Saud family through their campaigns to unify the Arabian Peninsula, culminating in the 1932 proclamation of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia.
adopted: The current design was standardized in 1973, fixing the proportions of a shahada-and-sword flag pattern already used by earlier 20th-century Saudi states.
layout: green field with inscription and sword
symbols: The Islamic shahada in white Arabic script across the center of the field.
A single white horizontal sword beneath the inscription, pointing toward the fly.
notes: The flag is never flown at half-mast and is not reproduced on merchandise or printed on both sides of some items, out of respect for the sacred inscription it carries.
disambiguation: This catalog's earlier 1902 Emirate of Nejd flag carries the same shahada but with two crossed swords rather than this flag's single sword.

context: Adopted after a 1969 military coup brought a government aligned with pan-Arab nationalism, replacing Sudan's first post-independence flag with colors shared by other Arab nationalist states.
adopted: Adopted in 1970, drawing on the Arab Liberation colors used by Egypt, Syria, Iraq, and Yemen, and replacing the blue-yellow-green flag flown since independence in 1956.
symbols: A green triangle at the hoist, its point reaching toward the fly, representing Islam and the country's fertile land.
disambiguation: Not to be confused with South Sudan's flag, which uses these same four colors plus blue and a gold star inside a blue triangle at the hoist.

context: Adopted at independence from France, sharing the pan-African green-yellow-red palette used by neighboring former French West African states while distinguishing itself with a central star.
adopted: Adopted in 1960 at independence, replacing the flag of the short-lived Mali Federation (Senegal's brief union with French Sudan), which had used a black kanaga figure instead of the star.
symbols: A single green five-pointed star centered on the yellow band.
disambiguation: Shares its green-yellow-red vertical tricolor with Mali and Guinea; distinguished from Mali's plain, unmarked tricolor by its central green star, and from Guinea's reversed color order of red-yellow-green.

context: Adopted just before self-government under British rule and retained through the brief merger with Malaysia and 1965 independence, designed to represent a multiracial society rather than any single ethnic group.
adopted: Adopted in 1959 for the new State of Singapore and kept unchanged through independence in 1965.
symbols: A white crescent moon opening toward the fly, paired with five small white five-pointed stars arranged in a circle, both set in the upper hoist area of the red band, representing a young nation and the ideals of democracy, peace, progress, justice, and equality.
disambiguation: The crescent-and-stars motif recalls Islamic symbolism seen on flags like Malaysia's, but Singapore's sits on a plain red-over-white field with no blue canton or extra stripes.

context: Adopted ahead of independence from the United Kingdom, chosen to represent the islands' land, sea, and sunshine along with the nation's main island groups.
adopted: Adopted in 1977, ahead of full independence in 1978.
symbols: A narrow yellow diagonal stripe running from the lower hoist to the upper fly, dividing the flag into a blue upper-hoist triangle and a green lower-fly triangle.
Five white five-pointed stars arranged in the blue triangle, representing the country's main island groups.
disambiguation: The diagonal yellow stripe over blue and green recalls Namibia's flag, but Namibia adds a sun disc and a white-bordered stripe rather than a cluster of stars.

context: Adopted at independence from Britain, the colors were chosen to represent the country's agriculture and mountains, unity and justice, and the natural harbor at Freetown.
adopted: Adopted in 1961 at independence.
disambiguation: Not to be confused with Nigeria's green-white-green vertical tricolor; Sierra Leone's is horizontal and ends in a distinct blue band rather than repeating green.

context: Adopted after the final dissolution of the Federal Republic of Central America, reviving that federation's blue-white-blue banner to signal El Salvador's continued attachment to the ideal of Central American unity.
adopted: Adopted in 1912, restoring the earlier Central American Federation's blue-white-blue tricolor that El Salvador had set aside for a period after the federation broke apart.
layout: horizontal tricolor with coat of arms
symbols: The national coat of arms, showing five volcanoes rising from the sea between two flags and encircled by a wreath and the words "REPUBLICA DE EL SALVADOR EN LA AMERICA CENTRAL", centered on the white band.
notes: A plainer civil version without the coat of arms is also used commercially.
disambiguation: Shares its blue-white-blue base and Central American Federation heritage with Guatemala's, Honduras's, and Nicaragua's flags; distinguished by its specific five-volcano coat of arms centered on the white band.

context: The white and light blue colors derive from the Apennine peaks and the sky as seen from Monte Titano, San Marino's historic mountain stronghold, reflecting its identity as one of the world's oldest surviving republics.
adopted: The white-and-blue pairing dates to the early 19th century, with the coat of arms added to the state flag in 1862.
layout: horizontal bicolor with coat of arms
symbols: The national coat of arms — three towers, each on its own peak of Monte Titano and topped with an ostrich plume, flanked by laurel and oak branches, above a banner reading "LIBERTAS" and beneath a crown — centered across both bands.
notes: The plain white-over-blue bicolor without the coat of arms serves as the civil flag; the version with the arms is the state flag.
disambiguation: Not to be confused with Argentina's or Nicaragua's light-blue-and-white flags, which use a different band order and different central emblems.

context: Adopted ahead of independence, the light blue field echoed the United Nations flag in recognition of the UN's role in overseeing the former Italian Somaliland's transition, while the star represented unity among Somali people beyond the new state's own borders.
adopted: Adopted in 1954 for the UN Trust Territory of Somaliland, and retained when it merged with British Somaliland to form the independent Somali Republic in 1960.
symbols: A single white five-pointed star centered on the field, its points originally meant to represent Somali-populated territories across the Horn of Africa.
disambiguation: Not to be confused with the United Nations flag, which shares a similar light blue but bears a white world-map-and-olive-branch emblem rather than a single star.

context: Following the breakup of Yugoslavia and the later split of Serbia and Montenegro, Serbia continued the Pan-Slavic tricolor tradition going back to the 19th-century kingdom, paired with a modernized coat of arms.
adopted: Adopted in its current precise form in 2010, refining the flag flown since Serbia's 2006 independence.
layout: horizontal tricolor with coat of arms
symbols: The Serbian coat of arms — a red shield bearing a white double-headed eagle beneath a crown, with a smaller crowned shield of a white cross and four firesteels on the eagle's breast — positioned toward the hoist, overlapping the top two bands.
notes: A plain tricolor without the coat of arms is also flown for civil use.
disambiguation: This catalog's earlier 1882 Kingdom of Serbia flag shares the same red-blue-white tricolor but carries an older, differently detailed coat of arms centered on the flag.

context: Adopted by the South Sudanese independence movement during its long struggle against the government in Khartoum, this flag became the new country's official flag after South Sudan seceded from Sudan following decades of civil war.
adopted: Adopted in 2005 as the flag of South Sudan's autonomous government under the peace agreement ending the civil war, and retained as the national flag upon full independence in 2011.
layout: horizontal field of stripes with triangle
symbols: A blue triangle at the hoist, its point reaching toward the fly, representing the Nile River and the country's waters.
A single gold five-pointed star centered in the blue triangle, representing unity among South Sudan's peoples.
disambiguation: Shares its black-red-green stripe colors and general layout with Sudan's flag, from which South Sudan seceded, but adds a blue hoist triangle with a gold star that Sudan's flag lacks.

context: Adopted at independence from Portugal, using the pan-African colors associated with liberation movements across the continent, with two stars representing the archipelago's two main islands.
adopted: Adopted in 1975 at independence.
symbols: Two black five-pointed stars set side by side on the yellow band, representing the islands of Sao Tome and Principe.
A red triangle at the hoist, its point reaching toward the fly.
disambiguation: Shares its green-yellow-green pan-African palette with several other former Portuguese and African territories' flags; distinguished by its red hoist triangle and exactly two stars, unlike, for example, Guinea-Bissau's single star on a divided field.

context: Adopted ahead of independence from the Netherlands, intended to represent the country's political spectrum and shared future rather than any single ethnic or political faction within Suriname's diverse society.
adopted: Adopted in 1975 at independence, replacing the flag used since the 1950s.
layout: horizontal field of stripes with star
symbols: A single large yellow five-pointed star centered on the red band, symbolizing unity and a golden future.
disambiguation: Not to be confused with Ghana's or Senegal's green-yellow-red combinations; Suriname's uses a wide red center band flanked by white and green with a single yellow star, a distinct five-stripe arrangement.

context: Adopted around the peaceful 1993 dissolution of Czechoslovakia, based on the Pan-Slavic tricolor tradition shared with other Slavic nations, distinguished by Slovakia's own coat of arms.
adopted: Adopted in 1992 ahead of full independence in 1993, adding the state's coat of arms to a plain Pan-Slavic tricolor to distinguish it from similar flags.
layout: horizontal tricolor with coat of arms
symbols: The Slovak coat of arms — a red shield bearing a white double cross rising from three blue hills — positioned off-center toward the hoist, overlapping all three bands.
disambiguation: Shares its white-blue-red tricolor and band order with Russia's and Slovenia's flags; distinguished from Russia's plain version by its coat of arms, and from Slovenia's by its different hill-and-cross emblem versus Slovenia's mountain-and-stars design.

context: Adopted as Slovenia moved toward independence from Yugoslavia, keeping the Pan-Slavic tricolor long associated with Slovene identity while replacing the socialist-era red star with a new coat of arms.
adopted: Adopted in 1991 at independence, replacing the star emblem carried on the flag during Slovenia's time within socialist Yugoslavia.
layout: horizontal tricolor with coat of arms
symbols: The Slovenian coat of arms — a shield showing white-outlined Mount Triglav above wavy blue lines representing rivers and the sea, with three gold six-pointed stars above — positioned in the upper hoist area, overlapping the white and blue bands.
disambiguation: Shares its white-blue-red tricolor with Russia's and Slovakia's flags; distinguished by its coat of arms sitting toward the upper hoist corner rather than centered, and by its distinctive mountain-and-stars design.

context: The blue-and-yellow cross design draws on centuries-old Swedish royal heraldic colors and the Nordic cross pattern shared across Scandinavia, a tradition tracing back to Denmark's flag.
adopted: The blue-and-gold cross design has centuries of heraldic history behind it; the flag's exact proportions were formally standardized by law in 1906.
disambiguation: Shares the Nordic cross layout with Denmark, Norway, Finland, and Iceland; distinguished from all of them by its blue field and gold, rather than white, red, or light blue, cross.

context: Adopted shortly before independence from Britain, based on a royal Swazi military flag presented decades earlier, giving the new state's flag strong traditional and monarchical symbolism distinct from many other African independence-era designs.
adopted: Adopted in 1968 at independence, based on a flag presented by King Sobhuza II to Swazi regiments in 1941.
layout: horizontal field of stripes with central emblem
symbols: A large Nguni war shield, black over white, centered on the red band.
Two spears and a feather-tasseled staff laid horizontally behind the shield.
notes: The shield and weapons are traditional Swazi royal and military regalia rather than a modern coat of arms.
disambiguation: Not to be confused with other southern African flags bearing shields, such as Kenya's, which sets crossed spears and a shield over a black-red-green field rather than this flag's blue-yellow-red base.

context: Adopted after a change of government ended one-party rule, the diverging bands radiating from the lower hoist were designed to represent a dynamic, forward-looking nation entering a new democratic era.
adopted: Adopted in 1996, replacing the flag used since independence from Britain in 1976.
disambiguation: Its fan of five diagonal bands radiating from the lower hoist is a distinctive layout not closely shared by any other national flag, avoiding confusion with conventional tricolors or bicolors.

context: After the fall of the Assad government in December 2024, Syria's new transitional authorities adopted the green-white-black flag with three red stars that had for years been used by the political opposition and, before that, by the independent Syrian Republic in the mid-20th century.
adopted: Adopted as Syria's flag following the Assad government's collapse in December 2024, restoring a design flown by Syrian opposition groups since the 2011 uprising; it replaced the red-white-black flag with two green stars used by the preceding Ba'athist-era government.
symbols: Three red five-pointed stars in a row, centered on the white band.
notes: This flag was flown for years by the Syrian opposition and diaspora before becoming the state's official flag again.
disambiguation: Not to be confused with the preceding Ba'athist-era Syrian flag, also red-white-black but bearing only two green stars, or with Iraq's similarly-colored tricolor, which carries script rather than stars.

context: Adopted at independence from France, the blue, yellow, and red were chosen to represent the sky and hope, the sun and desert, and unity and sacrifice, respectively.
adopted: Adopted in 1959 ahead of full independence in 1960.
disambiguation: Nearly identical to Romania's blue-yellow-red vertical tricolor, differing only in the exact shade of blue; also similar to Moldova's and Andorra's tricolors, which add a coat of arms that Chad's flag lacks.

context: Adopted ahead of independence from French trusteeship, the alternating green and gold stripes represented Togo's regions and the values of labor and faith, unified under a single red canton and star.
adopted: Adopted in 1960 at independence.
layout: horizontal field of stripes with canton
symbols: A white five-pointed star centered on the red canton in the upper hoist corner.
disambiguation: Not to be confused with Liberia's red-and-white striped flag with a blue canton and single star; Togo's uses green-and-yellow stripes with a red, not blue, canton.

context: Adopted during World War I as King Rama VI sought a flag more in keeping with international conventions, and added a fifth color, blue, to express solidarity with the Allied powers.
adopted: Adopted in 1917, replacing an earlier red-and-white striped flag that had itself briefly replaced the older flag bearing a white elephant emblem.
disambiguation: This catalog's earlier 1855 Siamese flag carries a white elephant emblem on a plain red field; the modern Trairanga replaces that entirely with five plain bands and a wide central blue stripe.

context: Adopted after independence from the Soviet Union, drawing on the red-white-green color association widespread in Persianate Central Asian symbolism, distinguished by a crown-and-stars emblem representing national sovereignty.
adopted: Adopted in 1992, replacing the Tajik Soviet Socialist Republic's red flag, amid the civil war that followed independence.
symbols: A gold crown centered on the white band, arched above by seven small gold five-pointed stars representing unity among Tajikistan's peoples.
disambiguation: Not to be confused with Hungary's or Bulgaria's red-white-green tricolors, which carry no crown-and-stars emblem and use a different stripe order.

context: Adopted shortly after independence from the Soviet Union, the flag's decorative vertical band reproduces traditional Turkmen carpet-weaving patterns associated with the country's major tribal confederations, expressing a distinctly Turkmen national identity.
adopted: Adopted in 1992, with the decorative stripe later modified in 1997 and 2001 to add further carpet motifs; the crescent and stars were part of the original 1992 design.
layout: field with vertical band and canton emblem
symbols: A white crescent moon opening toward the fly, with five white five-pointed stars arranged in an arc, both in the upper hoist area of the green field.
A vertical decorative stripe near the hoist containing traditional carpet-gul medallions in red, gold, and other colors, representing Turkmenistan's major tribes.
disambiguation: Not to be confused with other Central Asian green-and-crescent flags such as Azerbaijan's; Turkmenistan's is distinguished by its ornate vertical carpet-pattern stripe near the hoist, unique among national flags.

context: Adopted upon Timor-Leste's 2002 restoration of independence, reviving the flag briefly used in 1975 during Timor-Leste's short-lived declaration of independence from Portugal before Indonesia's invasion and subsequent occupation.
adopted: Originally adopted in 1975 at the first, short-lived declaration of independence; readopted in 2002 when Timor-Leste achieved full independence after a UN-supervised transition following the end of Indonesian rule.
symbols: A black triangle at the hoist bearing a single white five-pointed star, representing the path to enlightenment amid the struggle for independence.
A larger yellow triangle overlaid at the hoist, extending further toward the center of the field, representing traces of colonialism in Timor-Leste's history.
disambiguation: The black-and-yellow hoist triangles over red recall Mozambique's or Angola's liberation-movement-derived flags in spirit, but Timor-Leste's uses a single white star rather than any tool, gear, or crossed-weapon emblem.
assetWarning: The image file is a geometric construction/proportion diagram (with grid lines, measurement numbers, and an angle formula "theta = arctan(4/9) ~ 23.96 degrees" overlaid on the design) rather than a clean rendering of the flag. The underlying design elements — red field, black hoist triangle with white star, yellow overlaid triangle — are still identifiable and match Timor-Leste's actual flag, but the asset should ideally be replaced with a standard flag graphic.

context: Adopted under King George Tupou I as Tonga consolidated a unified constitutional kingdom, drawing on Christian symbolism to reflect Tonga's status as a Christian nation.
adopted: Adopted in 1875 alongside Tonga's constitution, which protects the design from ever being altered.
symbols: A red Greek cross, its arms not reaching the edges, centered within a white canton in the upper hoist corner.
notes: Tonga's constitution specifically forbids ever changing this flag's design.
disambiguation: Not to be confused with the Red Cross emblem's flag, a plain red cross on white with no red field, or with Georgia's flag, which places several small crosses across a mostly white field rather than a single canton cross on red.

context: Adopted ahead of independence from Britain, the diagonal design was chosen to be dynamic and distinct from the horizontal or vertical stripes common on other Caribbean flags, symbolizing the sun, sea, and the peoples of the twin-island nation.
adopted: Adopted in 1962 at independence.
disambiguation: Its black diagonal band edged in white and running from upper hoist to lower fly across a red field is a distinctive layout not closely shared by any other national flag.

context: Adopted under the Bey of Tunis during Ottoman suzerainty, echoing the Ottoman crescent-and-star tradition within a white disc reminiscent of Ottoman naval ensigns, and retained essentially unchanged through the French protectorate and into independence.
adopted: Adopted in 1831 under Hussein II Bey; formally confirmed as the national flag when Tunisia gained independence from France in 1956.
layout: red field with disc and symbol
symbols: A white disc centered on the red field, containing a red crescent moon opening toward the fly and a red five-pointed star at its center.
disambiguation: Not to be confused with the Ottoman Empire's or Turkey's flags, which place a plain crescent and star directly on a red field without the enclosing white disc.

context: The Turkish flag continues the crescent-and-star tradition of the late Ottoman Empire, retained essentially unchanged as the Ottoman state gave way to the modern Republic of Turkey after World War I.
adopted: The Ottoman-era design was formally standardized in 1936 by the young Republic, fixing the exact proportions and placement of a symbol already flown for decades before.
symbols: A white crescent moon opening toward the fly, with a white five-pointed star near the hoist side of the crescent's opening.
disambiguation: Nearly identical to this catalog's Ottoman Empire flag, from which it descends directly; the modern flag standardizes proportions the Ottoman-era flag left more variable, and it differs from Tunisia's flag, which encloses its crescent and star inside a white disc.

context: Adopted at independence from Britain, retaining the Union Jack in the canton to reflect continued Commonwealth ties while nine stars, arranged to mirror the geographic layout of Tuvalu's islands, mark the new nation's identity.
adopted: Adopted in 1978 at independence; briefly replaced by a different design in the mid-1990s before this flag was restored in 1997.
symbols: A Union Jack in the canton, occupying the upper hoist quarter.
Nine small yellow five-pointed stars scattered across the fly half of the field, arranged in the geographic pattern of Tuvalu's nine main islands.
disambiguation: Shares its light blue field and Union Jack canton with several other former British Pacific territories' flags, such as Fiji's; distinguished by its scattered nine-star pattern rather than a coat of arms or single emblem in the fly.

context: Following the Republic of China government's retreat to Taiwan at the end of the Chinese Civil War in 1949, this flag continued to represent the Republic of China as it administered Taiwan and outlying islands, though today most of the international community recognizes the People's Republic of China rather than the ROC.
adopted: This is the same Blue Sky, White Sun, and a Wholly Red Earth flag adopted by the Nationalist government in 1928 (catalogued separately for that mainland era); it has continued in use on Taiwan without interruption since the ROC government relocated there in 1949.
symbols: A white twelve-pointed sun centered in a blue canton occupying the upper hoist quarter.
notes: Its official status is politically contested: it is not recognized by the People's Republic of China or, formally, in many international venues, though it remains Taiwan's flag domestically.
aliases: Blue Sky, White Sun, and a Wholly Red Earth
disambiguation: Same design lineage as this catalog's 1928 Nationalist Republic of China flag; distinguished today mainly by context, since it now represents only Taiwan and nearby islands rather than mainland China.

context: Formed by combining elements of the flags of Tanganyika and Zanzibar following their 1964 union, blending Tanganyika's green-black-green and gold with Zanzibar's blue to represent the merged state.
adopted: Adopted in 1964 upon the union of Tanganyika and Zanzibar forming Tanzania.
disambiguation: Not to be confused with the Solomon Islands' or Namibia's diagonally divided flags, which use blue-and-green fields split by a single yellow stripe rather than Tanzania's black band bordered in yellow.

context: Adopted at independence, based on the flag of the Uganda People's Congress party that led the country to independence, with the crested crane chosen as a national emblem already associated with colonial-era Uganda.
adopted: Adopted in 1962 at independence from Britain.
layout: horizontal field of stripes with central emblem
symbols: A white disc centered on the flag, containing a grey crowned crane standing in profile with one leg raised, wearing its natural golden crest.
disambiguation: Not to be confused with other black-yellow-red striped African flags, a fairly common pan-African-adjacent palette; uniquely identifiable by the centered crested crane emblem.

context: The blue-and-yellow bicolor draws on medieval heraldic colors associated with the historic Kingdom of Galicia-Volhynia and was flown by short-lived Ukrainian states in the early 20th century before being suppressed under Soviet rule.
adopted: Readopted in 1992 shortly after Ukraine's independence from the Soviet Union, restoring a design used briefly by Ukrainian governments around 1917-1920 and again during the 1991 independence movement.
disambiguation: A simple two-color flag that does not closely resemble other national flags in layout; distinguished from Sweden's or Palau's blue-and-yellow combinations by having no cross or disc, just two plain horizontal bands.

context: Adopted after Uruguay's independence movement separated the country from both Brazil and the United Provinces, the nine stripes represent the nine original departments of the new state, with a sun emblem borrowed from Argentina's revolutionary iconography reflecting shared origins in the wars against Spanish rule.
adopted: Adopted in 1828 following Uruguay's independence, with the stripe count fixed at nine in 1830.
layout: horizontal field of stripes with canton
symbols: The Sun of May, a golden sun face with alternating straight and wavy rays, centered in the white canton in the upper hoist corner.
disambiguation: Shares the Sun of May emblem with Argentina's flag, but Uruguay's places the sun in a canton over striped bands rather than centered on a plain light-blue-and-white field.

context: The stripes commemorate the original thirteen British colonies that declared independence in 1776, while the stars in the canton have been added over time to reflect new states joining the Union.
adopted: The stripe-and-star design dates to 1777; the current 50-star version was adopted in 1960 following Hawaii's admission as the 50th state.
layout: horizontal field of stripes with canton
symbols: Fifty small white five-pointed stars arranged in rows in the blue canton, one for each state.
disambiguation: Its combination of thirteen horizontal stripes with a starred blue canton is unique among national flags, though the general canton-and-stripes concept has inspired other flags such as Liberia's, which uses a single star rather than fifty.

context: Adopted after independence from the Soviet Union, drawing on Turkic and Islamic symbolism alongside colors representing the sky, water, and purity, a clear break from the Uzbek Soviet Socialist Republic's red banner.
adopted: Adopted in 1991 at independence.
symbols: A white crescent moon opening toward the fly, with twelve small white five-pointed stars arranged in rows, both in the upper hoist area of the blue band.
disambiguation: Not to be confused with Turkmenistan's green flag with a crescent and stars; Uzbekistan's uses a blue-white-green striped base rather than a plain green field.

context: Adopted upon the creation of the sovereign Vatican City State by the 1929 Lateran Treaty between the Holy See and the Kingdom of Italy, ending decades of dispute over the papacy's territorial status following Italian unification.
adopted: Adopted in 1929 with the Vatican City State's founding, based on the yellow-and-white papal colors already used by the Holy See.
symbols: The papal tiara (triple crown) above two crossed keys, one gold and one silver, joined by a red cord, centered on the white half of the flag.
disambiguation: Not to be confused with the Holy See's own flag, a related but formally distinct entity that uses an identical design; distinguished from other yellow-and-white flags by its unique crossed-keys-and-tiara emblem.

context: Adopted ahead of full independence from Britain, the three diamonds arranged in a "V" shape stand for Saint Vincent's name and the "Gems of the Antilles" nickname sometimes applied to the islands.
adopted: Adopted in 1985, modifying a flag first used since 1979 independence by rearranging the diamonds into a clearer V formation.
symbols: Three green diamonds arranged in a V-shaped pattern, centered on the yellow band.
disambiguation: Not to be confused with other Caribbean tricolors; the distinctive V-shaped arrangement of three diamonds on the yellow band is unique to this flag.

context: Based on the tricolor devised by independence leader Francisco de Miranda and later used by Simon Bolivar's forces, the flag's colors and star tradition are shared with Colombia and Ecuador as fellow successor states of Gran Colombia.
adopted: The tricolor dates to Venezuela's early 19th-century independence struggle; an eighth star was added in 2006 to honor a province omitted from earlier versions.
symbols: Eight white five-pointed stars arranged in an arc, centered on the blue band, representing the provinces that signed Venezuela's 1811 declaration of independence plus one added later.
notes: The state flag additionally bears the national coat of arms in the upper hoist area; a plainer version without the arms is used more generally.
disambiguation: Shares its yellow-blue-red tricolor with Colombia's and Ecuador's flags, all three descending from the same Gran Colombia design; Venezuela's is distinguished by its arc of white stars on the blue band, which the others lack.
