context: Adopted by the Viet Minh during the independence struggle against French colonial rule, the red field and star reflected the revolutionary communist movement led by Ho Chi Minh, and the flag was extended to the whole country after North Vietnam's 1975 victory in the Vietnam War.
adopted: Adopted in 1945 by the Democratic Republic of Vietnam (North Vietnam); became the flag of a reunified Vietnam in 1976 following the fall of South Vietnam.
symbols: A single large yellow five-pointed star, centered on the red field.
disambiguation: Shares a red-field-with-yellow-star theme with China's flag, but Vietnam's uses one large centered star rather than one large star accompanied by four smaller ones.

context: Adopted at independence from the joint British-French Condominium government known as the New Hebrides, the design draws on local Melanesian symbolism, including a curled boar's tusk, a traditional symbol of prosperity, and ferns representing peace.
adopted: Adopted in 1980 at independence.
symbols: A black horizontal Y-shaped band, outlined in yellow, running from the hoist to the center before splitting toward the upper and lower fly corners.
A black triangle at the hoist containing a yellow curled boar's tusk encircling two crossed green fern leaves.
disambiguation: Its Y-shaped black-and-yellow chevron over red and green fields is a unique layout among national flags, not closely resembling any other country's design.

context: Adopted under New Zealand administration ahead of independence, the blue canton and Southern Cross constellation situate Samoa among the Pacific nations that use this star pattern to mark their location under the southern sky.
adopted: Adopted in 1949 while still a New Zealand-administered trust territory, and retained upon full independence in 1962.
symbols: The Southern Cross constellation, rendered as five white five-pointed stars, within a blue canton occupying the upper hoist quarter.
disambiguation: Shares the Southern Cross motif with Australia's, New Zealand's, and Papua New Guinea's flags; Samoa's is distinguished by its plain red field, with no additional stripes or extra stars, behind the star-bearing canton.

context: Adopted after Kosovo's 2008 declaration of independence from Serbia, the design was chosen through an international competition to avoid symbols associated with any single ethnic group, aiming for a flag acceptable to Kosovo's Albanian, Serb, and other communities.
adopted: Adopted in 2008 at the declaration of independence.
symbols: A gold silhouette map of Kosovo's territory, centered on the field.
Six white five-pointed stars arranged in an arc above the map, representing Kosovo's major ethnic communities.
disambiguation: Its use of a national territorial outline map as the central emblem, rather than a cross, star field, or coat of arms, is unusual among national flags and readily distinguishes it from neighboring countries' designs.

context: Adopted upon the 1990 unification of North Yemen and South Yemen, using the plain Arab Liberation colors shared by both predecessor states' flags to symbolize the merger without favoring either side's more specific symbols.
adopted: Adopted in 1990 at Yemeni unification, combining the two Yemeni states' flags, both of which already used variants of this red-white-black tricolor.
disambiguation: Shares the plain red-white-black Arab Liberation tricolor with Egypt's, Syria's, and Iraq's flags absent their added emblems; Yemen's is distinguished by carrying no central emblem at all, unlike those other states' flags.

context: Adopted as South Africa transitioned from apartheid to democracy, deliberately created without conventional heraldic meaning attached to its specific colors, meant to represent convergence and unity among formerly divided groups within a single new nation.
adopted: Adopted in 1994 for South Africa's first democratic elections, replacing the apartheid-era orange-white-blue flag.
notes: The design's six colors and converging shape were intentionally left without official symbolic meanings assigned to specific colors, unlike many national flags.
disambiguation: This catalog's earlier 1928 Union of South Africa flag, an orange-white-blue tricolor with three small flags on the white band, was fully replaced by this entirely different Y-shaped six-color design in 1994.

context: Adopted at independence from Britain, the green field represents the country's natural resources and vegetation while the stripes recall the colors of the nationalist movement that led Zambia to independence, and the eagle symbolizes freedom rising above the nation's challenges.
adopted: Adopted in 1964 at independence.
layout: field with vertical stripes and emblem
symbols: An orange eagle in flight, wings spread, positioned above the stripes in the upper fly area.
Three vertical stripes, red, black, then orange, positioned toward the fly below the eagle.
disambiguation: Not to be confused with other green African flags; distinguished by its combination of a fly-side vertical stripe block with an eagle placed above, rather than within, the stripes.

context: Adopted at independence following the end of white-minority rule and the Rhodesian Bush War, combining pan-African colors with the Zimbabwe Bird, a soapstone carving motif from the ancient Great Zimbabwe ruins, to root the new state's identity in the region's precolonial heritage.
adopted: Adopted in 1980 at independence, replacing the flag of the short-lived Zimbabwe Rhodesia government.
layout: horizontal field of stripes with triangle
symbols: A white triangle at the hoist, its point reaching toward the fly, containing a red five-pointed star and, atop it, a gold Zimbabwe Bird, a stylized bird derived from soapstone carvings found at the Great Zimbabwe ruins.
disambiguation: Not to be confused with other pan-African-colored striped flags; uniquely identifiable by its white hoist triangle bearing the Zimbabwe Bird atop a red star.

context: The Taliban readopted this plain white flag upon retaking Kabul in August 2021, reviving the design their first Islamic Emirate flew domestically from 1996 to 2001.
adopted: Readopted in August 2021 with the fall of the Western-backed Islamic Republic; it directly continues the 1996-2001 design rather than introducing a new one.
symbols: The Shahada (the Islamic declaration of faith) rendered in black Thuluth-style Arabic calligraphy, centered on the white field.
notes: Not recognized by the United Nations, where Afghanistan's seat remains contested; the black-red-green tricolor (see AFG/default.png, 2004-2021) is still used by opposition and diaspora groups who reject the current government.
disambiguation: Not to be confused with the black-red-green tricolor of the 2004-2021 Islamic Republic, nor with plain black jihadist/battle banners sometimes flown by affiliated militant groups, which are a separate design tradition from this white state flag.

context: British India was governed directly under the Crown after the 1858 transfer of authority from the East India Company. It had no official national flag of its own; the plain Union Jack was flown for general state purposes across the territory.
adopted: Standardized in 1885 as the personal flag of the Governor-General and Viceroy of India, and flown until the Raj's dissolution in 1947.
layout: Union Jack defaced with a central crowned badge
symbols: A gold Tudor crown atop a circular blue riband encircling a silver seven-pointed star, surrounded by radiating gold sunburst rays -- the 'Star of India' badge of the Order of the Star of India, instituted in 1861.
notes: British India had no single official national flag, so this is used here as the closest real, sourceable representation of 'the British Raj' as a polity -- the personal flag of its head of government rather than a true state flag, following the same convention other historical strategy games use for the same gap.
disambiguation: Not to be confused with the plain Union Jack flown generally across British India, or with the Star of India as a standalone order/medal insignia rather than a flag.
